collections.notes:
README.md

# Alabama 2006 agriculture commissioner map

This reconstruction maps the two-candidate margin between Democrat Ron Sparks
and Republican Albert Lipscomb using the available county-level precinct
returns and Census 2000 voting-district geometry.

## Reconstruction

1. Parse Sparks and Lipscomb votes, total ballots, and an independent partisan
   fingerprint from the other statewide contests in each county workbook.
2. Match each 2006 geographic reporting unit directly to a Census 2000 VTD in
   the same county. The 2016 VEST bridge is no longer used.
3. Use county-local VTD codes where they agree, then normalized polling-place
   and locality names. Abbreviations and generic site terms such as “school,”
   “church,” and “fire station” are handled separately from locality names.
4. Use the other-contest fingerprint, Census 2000 Black VAP share, and a broad
   ballots-to-VAP plausibility check as soft corroborating evidence. The
   agriculture commissioner result is excluded from its own matching score.
5. Accept only assignments meeting the documented score and best-versus-second
   candidate gap rules. Multiple reporting boxes may sum to one VTD; unresolved
   returns are not forced onto a polygon.
6. Apply a separately maintained reviewed-alias table for independently
   verified polling-place relocations and consolidated reporting units. The
   consolidated Daphne return is split among its three applicable 2000 VTDs
   using Census 2000 VAP; Daphne High School remains separately reported.
7. Preserve every Census 2000 VTD as an independent output feature.

## Display geometry

The PNG and SVG use a display-only dissolve for subordinate Census suffix
fragments. A suffixed VTD is merged into an existing same-county parent when
the polling-place identity similarity is at least 0.82 or the suffix has zero
population. This removes visually distracting cuts such as Madison County's
`11-A`/`11-B`/`11-C`, `53-1`/`53-2`, and similar fragments. The analytical
GeoPackage and `precinct-results.csv` retain all 1,987 original VTD features.
Every display merge is listed in `render-geometry-crosswalk.csv`.

The direct crosswalk conserves accepted geographic votes exactly. It is a
derived analytical crosswalk, not an official November 2006 precinct-boundary
file. Demographics are a plausibility prior, never a rule that a precinct must
vote for one party. Gray VTDs represent unresolved or unavailable returns and
are preferable to invented matches.

At the requested broad-coverage setting, automatic tiers C-E are also enabled:

- Tier C uses an address- or POI-level geocode contained by one correct-county
  VTD.
- Tier D aggregates multiple reporting units associated with one target and
  identifies flexible sources for county residual balancing.
- Tier E uses locality/street containment and a county-wide residual optimizer
  combining name, independent partisan fingerprint, turnout capacity, and
  one-source-per-VTD coverage. Exact and reviewed matches remain fixed.

The analytical crosswalk assigns 99.42% of allocable geographic votes and
populates 1,773 of 1,987 original VTDs. For a visually complete map, the
rendering layer fills 209 remaining non-Coosa display units with the nearest
observed same-county margin. These units retain their inferred color but are
visibly hatched in the statewide map and all metro windows. The display values
are not written back as vote allocations and are audited separately.

## Missing geography

The supplied Coosa County workbook omits the agriculture commissioner contest.
Consequently, all 20 Coosa County Census 2000 VTDs are gray. Other VTDs may be
gray when the evidence does not identify a unique 2006 reporting unit.
Absentee and provisional votes are included in the statewide margin but are not
assigned to VTDs. Coverage figures are recorded in `map_spec.json`.

## Files

- `alabama-2006-agriculture-commissioner-margin-by-precinct.png`: web raster.
- `alabama-2006-agriculture-commissioner-margin-by-precinct.svg`: editable map.
- `alabama-2006-agriculture-commissioner.gpkg`: valid Census 2000 VTD geometry
  with allocated votes and margins.
- `precinct-crosswalk-audit.csv`: candidate scores, evidence components,
  confidence, relationship type, and review status for every 2006 unit.
- `vtd-area-allocation-audit.csv`: accepted direct assignments and weights. The
  historical filename is retained for compatibility; no area weights are used.
- `precinct-results.csv`: final VTD attributes.
- `map_spec.json`: reproducible analytical and visual specification.
- `render-geometry-crosswalk.csv`: original-to-display geometry relationship;
  it does not alter the analytical crosswalk or vote allocation.
- `render-margin-inference-audit.csv`: identifies allocated versus tier-E
  nearest-neighbor display margins.

The reviewed source-to-target decisions live in
`alabama/data/crosswalks/alabama-2006-to-2000-reviewed-aliases.csv`, separate
from both the raw returns and generated audit.

Historically corroborated geocodes and automatic iterative assignments live in
`alabama/data/crosswalks/alabama-2006-to-2000-geocoded-aliases.csv` and
`alabama/data/crosswalks/alabama-2006-to-2000-iterative-aliases.csv`.

# Alabama modeled Black turnout, 2008–2016

## Claim
This analysis estimates posterior mean Black general-election ballots as a share of Census Black-alone voting-age population for Alabama counties in 2008, 2010, 2012, 2014, and 2016.

## Sources
The model uses precinct/VTD ballots, Census racial voting-age population, and the 2024 Alabama county geometry used by the rendering script. The script records the 2010 VTD inputs for 2008–2014 and 2020 Census block inputs assigned to 2016 precincts.

## Method
`estimate-alabama-2008-2016-black-turnout.py` fits hierarchical Bayesian ecological inference, bounds racial turnout odds, and reconciles posterior estimates to complete county ballot totals. The map uses fixed 0–90 percent intervals and hatching for precinct ballot coverage below 50 percent or a 94 percent interval wider than 50 percentage points.

## Limitations
These are ecological estimates, not individual voter records or candidate-choice estimates. Boundary-crosswalk uncertainty is not fully represented in the intervals, and low-coverage or wide-interval counties are flagged rather than treated as precise observations.

README.md

# Alabama presidential swing, 2016–2024

This directory maps the change in Democratic two-party presidential vote share
from 2016 to 2024 on the 2024 statewide precinct geography.

## Measure

`swing_pp = 100 × [Harris / (Harris + Trump) − Clinton / (Clinton + Trump)]`

Positive values indicate movement toward Democrats and negative values indicate
movement toward Republicans. Third-party votes are excluded from both years.
Zero is a color-class boundary rather than the center of a neutral class, so
every nonzero swing receives a directional color. Intensity changes in
five-percentage-point intervals on either side of zero.

## Crosswalk

- A 2016 and 2024 precinct pair is exact when each is the other's largest
  spatial match and both polygon-overlap shares are at least 99 percent.
- Exact pairs retain the reported 2016 vote totals without interpolation.
- Changed 2016 precincts are allocated to 2024 precincts using the voting-age
  population at official 2020 Census block internal points.
- Allocation is restricted within county boundaries and each source precinct's
  weights sum to one.
- Polygon area is implemented as a documented fallback for zero-VAP source
  precincts. It was not invoked in the completed statewide crosswalk.
- Allocated Clinton and Trump totals reconcile exactly to the VEST source totals
  in every county.

The crosswalk-quality categories describe target precincts: exact geometry,
simple merge, split allocation, or complex many-to-many boundary change. They
are relationship categories, not statistical confidence intervals.

## Files

- `alabama-presidential-swing-2016-2024.png` and `.svg`: finished swing map.
- `alabama-presidential-swing-crosswalk-quality.png` and `.svg`: boundary-change
  diagnostic map.
- `alabama-presidential-swing-2016-2024.gpkg`: 2024 precinct polygons with both
  elections, reconstructed 2016 totals, swing, and crosswalk class.
- `alabama-2016-to-2024-precinct-crosswalk.csv`: source-target weights,
  overlap shares, methods, and allocated 2016 candidate votes.
- `crosswalk-audit.json`: statewide totals, weight checks, reconciliation error,
  and category counts.
- `swing-color-breaks.csv`: exact five-point map intervals and hex colors.

## Sources and limitations

Election results and precinct geometry come from the repository's VEST-derived
2016 and Alabama 2024 statewide precinct files. Allocation weights use the 2020
Census PL 94-171 P3 voting-age total and TIGER/Line tabulation-block internal
points. A block-point allocation is substantially preferable to polygon area,
but it cannot recover within-block residential or voter-distribution differences.
The quality map should accompany close interpretation of reconstructed areas.

Fort Rucker in Coffee County has zero two-party presidential votes in both
source years and is the sole precinct shown without a swing value.

# Alabama 2017 special Senate election on current congressional districts

Seven precinct maps show **Doug Jones versus Roy Moore on December 12, 2017**,
within the same current adopted-2026 congressional boundaries used for the
recent AL-02 map. These are historical election results on newer boundaries,
not congressional race results or forecasts.

Every image carries **Jackson Hannan**, **X @electionsjack**, and
**linkedin.com/in/jackson-hannan**, verified from the supplied
[personal branding reference](https://jacksonahannan.github.io/alabama-state-house-and-state-senate-model/index.html?model=headline&chamber=house&mode=probability&view=map).
The white editorial treatment and 10-point red/blue margin bands match the
recent AL-02 maps; the oxblood identity accent comes from the reference site.
Social links are visible in PNGs and additionally clickable in SVGs.

## Social images

Each standalone map is **2160 × 2700 pixels, 4:5 portrait, 240 dpi**, with a
district locator, relevant metro detail, a write-in share and explicit tie and
missing-data keys. PNGs have opaque white backgrounds. Editable SVGs retain text.

[Download all seven social PNGs](alabama-2017-seven-district-social-maps.zip) ·
[Seven-district overview](seven-district-overview.png)

The download includes the seven full-resolution PNGs and this README. It does
not include original source geometry, precinct datasets or derived data tables.
The overview is a thumbnail contact sheet; use the individual images for posts.

| District | PNG | SVG | Jones | Moore | Write-ins | Jones minus Moore |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| AL-01 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-01.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-01.svg) | 47.52% | 50.69% | 1.79% | −3.17 pp |
| AL-02 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-02.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-02.svg) | 55.48% | 43.46% | 1.07% | +12.02 pp |
| AL-03 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-03.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-03.svg) | 43.06% | 55.27% | 1.68% | −12.21 pp |
| AL-04 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-04.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-04.svg) | 30.72% | 67.65% | 1.63% | −36.93 pp |
| AL-05 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-05.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-05.svg) | 48.44% | 49.03% | 2.52% | −0.59 pp |
| AL-06 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-06.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-06.svg) | 45.98% | 51.69% | 2.33% | −5.71 pp |
| AL-07 | [PNG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-07.png) | [SVG](maps/alabama-2017-senate-current-cd-07.svg) | 71.53% | 27.55% | 0.91% | +43.98 pp |

Percentages use **all valid votes, including write-ins**. Jones and Moore alone
therefore do not sum to 100%. District totals and percentages are population
allocations of historical returns, not certified totals for the current districts.

## Data and method

Original source: **Voting and Election Science Team (2019), _2017 Precinct-Level
Election Results_, Harvard Dataverse V9,
[doi:10.7910/DVN/VNJAB1](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/VNJAB1)**. The
[UF Election Lab Alabama 2017 dataset page](https://election.lab.ufl.edu/dataset/al-2017-precinct-level-election-results/)
and [provider documentation](https://election.lab.ufl.edu/data-downloads/resultsdata/2017/precinct/documentation.txt)
identify the dataset and processing. The local archive's required shapefile
companions are hash-matched to the existing unpacked source before loading.

The provider documents countywide absentee/provisional allocation using each
candidate's precinct shares, along with some differences from certified canvass
returns. The maps use the published VEST values; no additional absentee
allocation or silent canvass adjustment is introduced here.

The **1,996 original precincts** are intersected with all seven districts in the
same supplied adopted-2026 plan as the recent AL-02 maps. Its internal file name
is `2023_CONG_LEGISLATIVE_PLAN.shp`; the current plan is documented in the
[Secretary of State district-map download](https://www.sos.alabama.gov/alabama-votes/state-district-maps).
The newer district boundaries did not govern the 2017 election.

Candidate votes are allocated among district intersections by **2020 Census
block voting-age population points** within each original precinct. This assumes
equal candidate preference and turnout within the parent precinct, and uses 2020
settlement patterns to approximate the location of 2017 voters. All 1,996 source
precincts have populated block support, so no nearest assignments or area
fallbacks were needed. Every precinct and all 67 county candidate totals are
conserved; the greatest numerical precinct error is below 5e-13 votes.

All **2,373 precinct/district pieces** retain the original parent precinct's
Jones–Moore margin for map coloring. Source shares are distinct from allocated
district vote counts. A known historical precinct ratio stays visible on an
uninhabited split piece even if its allocated count is zero. Ties receive a cream
fill with hatching; gray means genuine zero-valid-vote source geography. The sole
zero-valid-vote source feature is Coffee County's unassigned unit.

Reprojection to EPSG:5070 required 30 source geometry repairs; three repaired
collections included zero-area line remnants. Polygon components and all source
vote identities were retained. The total repair area effect was 1.436 m². No
simplification or snapping changes source coordinates. Small boundary-vintage
coverage differences are audited for every district; the largest is 0.0332 km²
in AL-07. Missing land or votes are not fabricated to conceal those differences.

## Source-versus-certified totals

The seven district allocations sum to the original VEST precinct totals:

| Category | VEST source conserved here | Certified canvass | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Doug Jones | 673,889 | 673,896 | −7 |
| Roy Moore | 651,983 | 651,972 | +11 |
| Write-ins | 22,877 | 22,852 | +25 |
| Total | 1,348,749 | 1,348,720 | +29 |

provides the canvass comparison. The provider documents county-specific
differences; preserving and disclosing the source avoids manufacturing corrected
precinct results. Neither a district allocation nor a VEST source sum is labeled
as a certified current-district canvass.

## Attribution and reproducibility

The [provider's precinct-data page](https://election.lab.ufl.edu/precinct-data/)
encourages election-result visualization and identifies its 2016–2020 data as
[CC BY-NC-ND 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).

# Alabama 2024 white-voter counterfactual

The education scenario models the 2024 Alabama presidential election if white
college graduates split 56 percent for Kamala Harris and 42 percent for Donald
Trump, while white non-college voters split 39 percent for Harris and 60 percent
for Trump. Each supplied split is normalized within the two-party vote.

The analysis keeps every precinct's total Harris-plus-Trump turnout unchanged.
White voter composition is estimated from 2019–2023 ACS citizen voting-age
population, distributed through populated 2020 Census blocks and calibrated so
each county reproduces Alabama's official 2024 white share of participating
voters. Existing white preference is anchored to the vote-weighted result in
precincts whose modeled electorate is at least 90 percent white. The statewide
nonwhite rate is then solved so the two modeled groups exactly reproduce the
actual Alabama result. White non-Hispanic bachelor's attainment comes from ACS
table C15002H. The scenario replaces only the two white education-group
preferences and holds estimated nonwhite preference constant.

This is an ecological counterfactual, not an identification of individual
voters or ballots. CVAP estimates have sampling error, county racial
participation categories are administrative classifications, and group voting
preferences are modeled from aggregate precinct returns.

Both variants use one shared nonlinear margin scale so the actual and modeled
panels remain comparable while close precincts receive more contrast. Breaks
are 0, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, and 100 points in either direction. The
ColorBrewer version changes only the palette to a conventional `RdBu` sequence.

Marques 90,890**, exactly **one vote** out of **181,781** hypothetical two-party
votes. Shares are 50.000275% and 49.999725%. The one-vote finish is a user-specified
calibration target, not a forecast or measured likelihood.

[PNG](alabama-2026-al2-figures-win.png) ·
[Editable SVG](alabama-2026-al2-figures-win.svg) ·
[Precinct data](data/precinct-results.csv) ·
[Summary](data/summary.json) ·
[Demographic support](data/demographic-support.csv) ·
[Sensitivity](data/assumption-sensitivity.csv) ·
[Audit](model-audit.json)

The map retains the latest Alabama governor polling map's typography, palette,
10-point margin bands, and white background, with a Montgomery precinct inset.
It uses the same supplied adopted-2026 AL-02 boundary as the earlier map. The
previous 59.5% Figures illustration is preserved at
`alabama/research/al2-figures-win-2026/previous-illustrative-scenario/`.

The [matching partisan primary comparison](../alabama-2026-al2-primary-comparison/alabama-2026-al2-primary-comparison.png)
uses the same precinct geometry, district population allocation, layout and
margin bands. It shows May party-primary ballots rather than a modeled
general-election candidate result.

The apparently missing precinct was **Sweet Pilgrim Church, Pike County
(AL26-1593)**. Its scenario result is **38–38**, and its May ballot result is
also tied, **24–24**. The polygon and counts are intact. Both maps now hatch
tied precincts and include separate legend keys for ties and no allocated
votes. The combined precinct polygons cover the adopted district apart from
34.303 square meters of microscopic projection-boundary artifacts; there is
no missing precinct geometry.

## A historically grounded turnout scale

The scenario starts from **2024 precinct presidential two-party vote totals**,
not May primary ballot counts. The current AL-02 population allocation estimates
289,860.671 Harris-plus-Trump votes in 2024 and 181,781.840 Flowers-plus-Ivey
governor votes in 2022. The latter is **62.7135%** of the former. These historical
votes are mapped onto common precinct geography; district splits remain estimates.

The total is the nearest odd integer to the 2022 benchmark: **181,781**. An odd
number is necessary for a two-candidate win by exactly one vote. This is a
historical midterm turnout scenario, not a numerical prediction of 2026 turnout.
It avoids the earlier arbitrary +20%/−30% race-specific turnout multipliers.

The statewide [Secretary of State comprehensive turnout series](https://www.sos.alabama.gov/sites/default/files/election-data/2026-07/Comprehensive%20Voter%20Turnout%201986-2024.pdf)
provides context: 1,423,409 ballots in 2022 versus 2,272,911 in 2024, about 62.6%.
Those statewide all-ballot counts differ from our district two-party contest
counts; neither denominator is substituted for the other.

## Electorate composition: six percentage points

The user confirmed **percentage points**, rather than six-percent relative
changes. Six points of the modeled electorate move from White to Black, with
residual Other unchanged:

| Group | Estimated 2024 district electorate | Scenario electorate | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Black | 35.9503% | 41.9503% | +6.0000 pp |
| White | 61.2181% | 55.2181% | −6.0000 pp |
| Other / unidentified residual | 2.8316% | 2.8316% | unchanged |

The 2024 district racial electorate is **modeled**, not directly observed.
For each county, iterative proportional fitting preserves each precinct's actual
2024 two-party vote total and matches the county's official racial participation
proportions. Census CVAP fractions seed the allocation. The official
[2024 racial-participation PDF](https://www.sos.alabama.gov/sites/default/files/election-data/2025-10/2024%20General%20Election%20Participation%20by%20Race.pdf)
counts registered race categories. White, Black, and residual
`all ballots − White ballots − Black ballots` are used; unidentified alone is
not treated as the entire residual. SOS registered race definitions differ from
Census non-Hispanic race, so this allocation is an ecological approximation.
Racial-report totals also differ slightly from the state's all-ballot turnout
series. Only the report's county proportions are used; 2024 precinct results set
the row totals.

The six-point change is the user's AL-02 scenario assumption. Georgia's available
matched early-vote snapshot was directionally similar, but neither it nor the
Louisiana material verified an exact six-point change in a final electorate.
See the [source findings](../../alabama/research/al2-figures-win-2026/findings.md).

Within the White electorate, BA+ turnout receives relative weight 1.00;
noncollege turnout receives 0.97 at the dense endpoint and 0.90 at the sparse
endpoint, with continuous interpolation. The sparse-settlement proxy is
`r = 1/(1 + source-precinct voting-age residents per km² / 100)`.
This is density, not a Census rural classification; full source-precinct area
includes water. White cells are then normalized jointly to the required 55.2181%
White electorate. Black and residual cells are separately normalized to their
targets. Thus the education/density profile cannot accidentally change the
specified district race shares. Shares describe electorate composition, not
turnout rates among registered voters. Absolute midterm turnout is lower than
2024 even though Black share increases.

## General-election support and the May geographic signal

Raw May party-primary ballot shares are not general-election candidate
preferences. A direct transfer produced the earlier implausibly large win.
The revision anchors local support to the **2024 presidential two-party share**
and uses May participation as a bounded geographic update:

1. Compute half-vote-smoothed Democratic shares for 2024 and May 2026.
2. Regress their log-odds difference on an intercept and modeled 2024 Black and
   residual voter shares, weighted by district May ballots. Remove this broad
   composition association.
3. Stabilize the residual with `May ballots / (May ballots + 50)`, cap it at
   ±0.75 log-odds, center it on 2024 district turnout, and cap again.
4. Add **20%** of the residual to 2024 presidential log-odds. The maximum local
   update is therefore ±0.15 log-odds. This preserves a modest May local pattern
   without importing the primary's selected electorate wholesale.

The 20% transfer strength and stabilization/cap are declared modeling choices,
not independently estimated candidate effects. No Jones-specific crossover or
2024 old-district congressional result is substituted for Figures's 2026 race.

Four latent cells split each precinct: White noncollege, White BA+, Black, and
Other. Initial Democratic support priors are 10%, 25%, 95%, and 50%. A separate
precinct intercept adjusts those priors to reproduce the combined 2024-plus-May
geographic support baseline. Neither the initial priors nor the final cell
probabilities are observed individual voter choices.

After the turnout changes, the model has **Figures 47.7769% before the additional
support shift**. One scalar log-odds shift is then fitted to the one-vote target.
Its loadings are 1.30 for White BA+, 0.80–1.20 for White noncollege from dense to
sparse, 0.35 for Black, and 0.80 for Other. This allows larger White college gains,
modest White noncollege gains, and a small change within already strong Black
support. The fitted scalar is **0.269640 log-odds**.

| Group | Support before fitted shift | Final Figures support | Support change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Black | 93.16% | 93.66% | +0.50 pp |
| White BA+ | 22.60% | 28.53% | +5.93 pp |
| White noncollege | 9.21% | 11.50% | +2.29 pp |
| Other | 47.14% | 51.76% | +4.62 pp |

Both columns average over the **same revised electorate**, so their difference
isolates the support adjustment. These are plausible illustrative support levels,
not candidate-specific polling estimates. Geography produces different support
within each demographic cell across precincts. The model assumes a common
structured support shift; it does not fit independent precinct swings.

## Exact integer conservation

Hamilton apportionment distributes the odd turnout total across precincts,
breaking tied fractional remainders by stable precinct ID. A second demographic
balancing step preserves those integer precinct totals while recovering the
continuous race-share targets. Latent racial cell weights may be fractional;
they are ecological estimates rather than counts of identified voters.

Support is calibrated on those turnout totals to an expected Democratic count of
90,891. Democratic precinct counts are rounded by largest remainders to sum to
90,891; Republican counts are each precinct's integer turnout minus its
Democratic count. This guarantees 90,890 Republican votes, an exact one-vote
margin, and unchanged turnout in every precinct. Each candidate rounding error
is less than one vote per precinct. Precinct map margins use the final integer
counts, not unrounded model probabilities.

## Sensitivity and limitations

The sensitivity table holds the turnout total and White education/density
profile fixed, varies the White-to-Black composition transfer, and refits support
to the same one-vote target:

| Black-share increase | Figures before support shift | Required White BA+ support | Required White noncollege support |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 pp | 42.99% | 39.81% | 16.25% |
| 4 pp | 46.18% | 32.53% | 13.12% |
| 6 pp | 47.78% | 28.53% | 11.50% |
| 8 pp | 49.37% | 24.31% | 9.86% |

These alternatives describe the support needed to meet a fixed outcome; they
are not predictive probabilities or a confidence interval. Rurality, education,
county racial allocation, support priors, and the May transfer remain model
assumptions. Education is ACS age-25+ non-Hispanic White BA+ attainment used as a
proxy among voters. No claim is made to observe voter-level race or education.

The boundary is the supplied adopted-2026 plan, internally named the 2023
legislative plan, verified against the current
[state map download](https://www.sos.alabama.gov/alabama-votes/state-district-maps).
It extends from Montgomery toward Dothan and excludes Mobile. May absentee and
provisional ballots without residential geography are excluded from the primary
signal. The 2024 and historical 2022 data inherit their source's absentee and
historical-vintage allocation assumptions. Four materially split precincts use
2020 Census block VAP weights. There are 313 precincts with modeled votes plus
41 retained tiny, uninhabited boundary intersections. Existing projection repairs
and their sub-0.001-m² area effects remain audited.

## Rebuild and verification

From the repository root:

```bash
./.venv/bin/python scripts/estimate-alabama-2026-al2-figures-win.py
./.venv/bin/python scripts/render-alabama-2026-al2-figures-win-map.py
./.venv/bin/python scripts/estimate-alabama-2026-al2-figures-win.py --finalize
./.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_alabama_2026_al2_figures_win.py tests/test_alabama_2026_governor_rendering.py
./.venv/bin/election-maps validate-outputs outputs/alabama-2026-al2-figures-win
```

Sources are identified and hashed in `provenance.json`; the local GeoPackage is a
rebuild product. The PNG is 3360 × 2880 at 240 dpi and the SVG preserves text.

The map shows where Democratic or Republican first-round primary ballots predominated within Alabama's adopted Congressional District 2.

# Alabama Governor 2026 according to current polling

These hypothetical Jones–Tuberville maps condition on the three unique statewide polls plus historical voting and the May nominee results. **The statewide poll totals are exact; the demographic and media-market crosstabs are soft evidence.** They are not a claim that every published crosstab is simultaneously correct. District counts refer to the governor vote, not actual legislative race winners.

A material limitation is the age18–29 crosstab: the central model estimates about51% Jones, versus75–77% among decided/allocated voters in the source poll. The difference is24–26 percentage points. This revision prioritizes observed candidate geography and does not resolve that conflict. A wider age-effect sensitivity reaches about63% without changing the proportional37 House/10 Senate count. Full residuals and all sensitivities are retained below.

| Scenario | Jones statewide | Tuberville statewide | House Jones / Tuberville | Senate Jones / Tuberville |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Proportional statewide allocation | 43.25% | 56.75% | 37 / 68 | 10 / 25 |
| Equal statewide allocation | 43.78% | 56.22% | 37 / 68 | 10 / 25 |

Open [proportional overview](maps/proportional-overview.png) or [equal-allocation overview](maps/equal-overview.png). Both sets include all1,947 precincts,67 counties,105 House and35 Senate districts, as PNG and editable SVG. The equal/proportional rules describe allocation of the **pooled statewide undecided total**. Historical subgroup adjustments mean undecideds are no longer mechanically assigned50/50 inside every demographic category. This added historical assumption is explicit.

Presentation uses an original editorial layout: white paper, a compact Nimbus Sans title and scenario subtitle, a thin header rule, and an unboxed vote table. Candidate colors identify data; the hypothetical-estimate label remains visible. [VoteHub](https://votehub.com/polls/) and [The Argument](https://www.theargumentmag.com/) are presentation references, without reproducing their branding. This presentation revision does not change the underlying estimates or district counts.

The [interactive GitHub Pages dashboard](https://jacksonahannan.github.io/alabama-governor-2026-polling/) includes both scenarios and all four layers, county/district-to-precinct drilldown, search, shareable selections, historical comparisons and demographic context. Legislative drilldown clips precinct shapes to the selected district and displays candidate vote weights allocated by the existing 2020 block-VAP crosswalk; percentages retain the uniform within-precinct preference assumption, and district totals remain unchanged. It serves the October24 model snapshot and does not automatically collect new polls. The [public repository](https://github.com/JacksonAHannan/alabama-governor-2026-polling) contains only the reviewed static website. Rebuild/export/publishing instructions are in the [dashboard README](../../alabama/governor-2026-poll-dashboard/README.md).

| Geography | Proportional | Equal allocation |
|---|---|---|
| Precinct | [PNG](maps/proportional/precinct.png) / [SVG](maps/proportional/precinct.svg) | [PNG](maps/equal/precinct.png) / [SVG](maps/equal/precinct.svg) |
| County | [PNG](maps/proportional/county.png) / [SVG](maps/proportional/county.svg) | [PNG](maps/equal/county.png) / [SVG](maps/equal/county.svg) |
| State House | [PNG](maps/proportional/house.png) / [SVG](maps/proportional/house.svg) | [PNG](maps/equal/house.png) / [SVG](maps/equal/house.svg) |
| State Senate | [PNG](maps/proportional/senate.png) / [SVG](maps/proportional/senate.svg) | [PNG](maps/equal/senate.png) / [SVG](maps/equal/senate.svg) |

## Madison, Huntsville and the requested districts

The May returns confirm Jones outpolled Tuberville in HD-10,HD-25,SD-2 andSD-7. The party-primary statewide comparison was Republican+14.96 points; the nominee-only comparison was Tuberville+19.05. These are different denominators. Census white BA+ proxies among white adults in the four districts range from50.18% to59.97%.

| District | Jones2020 on current boundaries | Jones May nominee share | Previous proportional model | Revised proportional | Revised equal |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| HD-10 | 52.59% | 57.59% | 48.79% | 61.55% | 62.50% |
| HD-25 | 48.34% | 54.29% | 47.31% | 59.09% | 60.07% |
| SD-2 | 52.12% | 59.08% | 50.71% | 61.26% | 62.16% |
| SD-7 | 48.26% | 50.71% | 45.51% | 55.43% | 56.37% |

Historical and May district votes are population-crosswalk estimates, not official district canvasses. [Focused comparison](data/madison-focus-comparison.csv) includes Census composition and modeled race/education diagnostics; [all140 districts](data/all-district-historical-comparison.csv) are retained. No named district overrides or preferred winners enter the model.

Madison County gave Jones48.78% in2020, versus Biden45.92% on the same day. Jones's2017 Madison share was58.73%, against a different opponent. The revised model gives Jones57.04% under proportional allocation and57.97% under equal allocation. The county's high education level is relevant, but statewide education averages alone cannot represent its local candidate history.

Past elections also show substantial variation: official2022 counts favored Republicans in all four districts, while Marilyn Lands won the2024 HD-10 special3725–2238. These are contextual checks, not copied2026 targets. [Huntsville research](../../alabama/research/governor-poll-scenario-2026/huntsville-history-review/findings.md) cites certified sources. NASA Marshall's technical presence is documented context; the model assigns no invented partisan coefficient to its employees.

## Historical Black voting and the previous underprediction

[CNN's2017 transcript](https://transcripts.cnn.com/show/cnr/date/2017-12-14/segment/17) reports96% Black support for Jones. TableG in the [2024 expert-report filing](https://vhdshf2oms2wcnsvk7sdv3so.blob.core.windows.net/thearp-media/documents/AL_221-cv-1530_384.pdf), report page32/PDF page129, transcribes2020 exit polling as90% Jones and89% Biden among Black voters. The original2020 interactive survey table was inaccessible, so this is labelled an expert transcription, not direct microdata or ballot-record racial counts. The96%2017 figure concerns Moore and is not a2026 target.

The separate geographic check is stronger than a blanket racial adjustment: precincts at least90% Black by the Census CVAP proxy gave Harris94.89% in2024 and Jones97.26% in2020, but the previous proportional model estimated87.99%. The revised proportional result is96.76%. At the80% Black threshold, observed Harris was92.28%, Jones2020 was94.76%, old model84.78%, revised94.64%. **These are precinct aggregates, not observations of individual Black preferences.** Turnout and resident racial composition differ.

The individual-cell model uses90% historical Black support as an added prior with an analyst-selected five-point scale. The current Cygnal79 Jones/11 Tuberville/10 undecided remains soft evidence: its two-party Jones target is87.78% proportional and84% equal. The model does not silently relabel those source figures. Fitted statewide Black-cell Jones support is90.36% proportional and89.95% equal, compared with the previous87.58% and83.89%. The larger Madison correction also reflects restored candidate and education geography; it cannot all be attributed to Black support.

See [Black-precinct comparison](data/black-precinct-historical-comparison.csv), [latent race/education table](data/proportional-latent-race-education.csv), and the calibration CSV. Latent allocations are assumptions constrained by geographic totals, not identified individual voting behavior.

## Reproducible geographic prior

1. Start with smoothed2024 Harris–Trump precinct log-odds. Add Jones's observed2020 advantage over Biden in log-odds from the same precinct geography. The crossover is stabilized by `n/(n+50)`, where n is the smaller2020 two-party contest total. Candidate shares use `(D+0.5)/(D+R+1)` smoothing. This carries Jones's actual local matchup geography onto the later presidential pattern.
2. Calculate May Jones-versus-Tuberville log-odds minus that complete historical anchor. Regress the difference on an intercept, Black CVAP share and residual-race CVAP share, weighted by May nominee votes. Remove only that descriptive race-composition association. It is not a causally identified primary-turnout adjustment. Education, age and regional patterns are not stripped out.
3. Stabilize the remaining May update by `n/(n+50)`, center its2024-turnout-weighted mean at zero, and transfer one quarter of it into the prior. Quarter strength is an assumption, tested against zero and one half. [Geographic prior table](data/candidate-history-geographic-prior.csv) preserves all input shares, crossover, adjustment and residual terms.
4. Use four race/education classes by five ages inside each precinct. White education composition comes from Census C15002H BA+ age25+; age comes from B01001; race comes from2019–2023 CVAP. The initial white level uses the Cygnal white target, with conditional college/noncollege odds ratio2.1 from the historical [Alabama2024 Fox/NORC survey](https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2024/general-results/state/alabama). Black starts at the90% historical prior and residual Other at an explicitly assumed50%.
5. Solve a separate precinct intercept so the20 latent cells reproduce **each geographic prior exactly**. Thus the education seed cannot initially erase local historical support or add a second education boost on top of it. Race/education and age independence within precinct remains an unobserved joint-distribution assumption.
6. Fit zero-centered race, age and approximate-market adjustments with an intercept that enforces the statewide pool exactly. Soft mismatch scales are White6 points, Black8, age10, market7, plus the historical Black five-point scale. Coefficient regularization scales are0.35 for the Black contrast and age effects,0.50 Other,0.25 markets. These are analyst regularization choices, **not survey standard errors or confidence intervals**.

[Calibration and residuals](data/calibration-and-education-estimates.csv) report every source target and fitted margin. Only statewide is hard. The model intentionally does not claim to match all crosstabs; the young-voter departure at the beginning of this document is substantial. The wider-age and age-poll-omitted sensitivities make that choice reviewable.

The modeled statewide white-college Jones share is40.71% proportional and41.86% equal, versus20.82%/21.63% among white noncollege cells. These statewide averages are not imposed uniformly on Madison: the local historical intercepts retain its different geography. Census education rates include adults25+, including noncitizens, and are applied as proxies within white CVAP18+; neither they nor the model are a voter file.

## Poll arithmetic, source geography and sensitivity

The duplicate ADN link is counted once. Cygnal n500 and Lowry n600 likely voters plus Napolitan n800 registered voters are sample-size weighted without recency/quality adjustment. Complete rows are renormalized for rounding (Cygnal100.1, Napolitan99). Lowry's precise original release, not the earlier rounded article, supplies39.4/50.8/5.7 undecided/4.1 Burnette. Original Napolitan separates other-candidate and nonvoting choices from unsure. With pooled D,R,U, proportional is `D/(D+R)` and equal is `(D+U/2)/(D+R+U)`. Other/nonvoting categories are excluded, not allocated as undecideds. These mixed samples do not yield a defensible combined sampling-error interval. [Source findings](../../alabama/research/governor-poll-scenario-2026/findings.md) and [arithmetic CSV](data/poll-aggregation.csv) provide original links.

Historical VEST/RDH counts are mapped to1,947 current reporting precincts with2020 Census block-VAP weights, conserving every source county/state total. The2017 archive lacks a processing README and its source-universe totals are not asserted to be exact certified totals. The2020 source already allocates absentee/provisional votes; they are not added twice. The2022 comparison needs five county-constrained nearest block assignments (33 VAP, maximum29.21m);2016/2017/2020 need none. [Historical source audit](../../alabama/data/governor-poll-scenario-2026/historical-baseline/historical-baseline-audit.json) and [findings](../../alabama/research/governor-poll-scenario-2026/historical-baseline-findings.md) record source keys, repairs, hashes and vintages.

The May builder maps1,923 current primary features to1,947 target precincts without nearest or area fallback. It preserves365,408 Democratic,493,988 Republican,287,146 Jones and422,255 Tuberville governor votes, including explicitly allocated9070D/9320R countywide votes. Countywide votes are assigned by same-party election-day participation within county because home precincts are unknown. [May audit](../../alabama/data/governor-poll-scenario-2026/primary-baseline/baseline-audit.json) retains all counts and weights.

Relative turnout remains2024 Harris+Trump votes,2,235,028 statewide, not a2026 turnout forecast. `*_votes` in scenario outputs are weights in2024 vote units. All four geographies preserve their sums. Current legislative results use adopted2021 plans and within-precinct2020 block-VAP allocation, assuming equal preference/turnout across split parts. Processing uses EPSG:5070. Twenty-five zero-white education tracts and seven zero-VAP age tracts use documented county fallback; Fort Rucker alone has zero2024 vote weight and is drawn gray. [Census metadata](../../alabama/data/governor-poll-scenario-2026/demographics-metadata.json) supplies exact denominators and caveats.

The market proxy uses historical broadcaster county definitions; private2026 Cygnal memberships remain unavailable. The4 named markets do not absorb Dothan/Other. Colors and legend share seven10-point winner-margin bins; House/Senate maps draw district edges without county crosscuts or white seams.

## Exact arithmetic decomposition on eligible matched units

For precinct margin `m` in percentage points and precinct share `w` of the comparison set's two-party votes, aggregate margin is `M = Σ(w × m)`. The symmetric identity is:

`M26 − M24 = Σ[((w26+w24)/2) × (m26−m24)] + Σ[((m26+m24)/2) × (w26−w24)]`.

The first term is the midpoint-weighted change in precinct margins. The second is the effect of changed **geographic shares of recorded two-party vote volume**. This is an exact accounting identity, not a causal or voter-behavior model. A precinct's internal change can combine different voters, changing population, ballot choice and participation.

| Scope / 2026 race | Matched units | 2024 two-party votes | 2026 two-party votes | Aggregate margin change | Within-unit term | Geographic-weight term | Volume ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Alabama governor | 1823 | 1,926,048 | 1,481,535 | +27.380 pp | +21.988 pp | +5.392 pp | 0.7692 |
| Alabama Senate | 1823 | 1,926,048 | 1,479,269 | +21.776 pp | +16.445 pp | +5.331 pp | 0.7680 |
| CD5 House | 196 | 297,648 | 235,634 | +23.809 pp | +19.416 pp | +4.393 pp | 0.7917 |

The positive geographic-weight terms mean that units' changing shares of recorded vote volume contribute to the aggregate Democratic margin shift under this accounting convention. They do not establish a racial, age, income or individual-turnout explanation. The identity was numerically verified to an absolute tolerance of 1×10⁻¹⁰ percentage points before rounding.

It contains 865 statewide contest/unit ballot-accounting differences from the reported ballot-total rows; these remain unresolved. Full-race totals preserve reported administrative votes, while mapped comparisons exclude those votes. Matching relies on documented reporting-label/crosswalk evidence and assumed continuity, not legal certification of every precinct boundary. Excluded units may differ systematically from included units. No comparison here establishes that 2026 population or demographic composition was directly observed.



# What the demographic comparisons show

Numerical interpretation of the frozen November 17, 2026 meeting analysis. The source is `outputs/alabama-2026-jackson-meeting/demographic-strata.csv`, using the final crosswalk with **1,823 comparable statewide reporting units** and **196 whole reporting units in CD5**. These are observed election returns grouped by estimated resident composition. They do not measure how individual demographic groups voted or identify demographic causes.

## Overall movement and the office difference

Within the same 1,823 matched statewide units, Democratic two-party vote share was **33.85% for president in 2024, 47.54% for governor in 2026, and 44.74% for Senate in 2026**. That is a change in D–R margin of **+27.4 percentage points for governor and +21.8 for Senate**. A D–R margin change is twice the corresponding change in Democratic two-party share.

Within the 196 CD5 whole reporting units, the 2024 Democratic presidential share was **34.55%**. The 2026 shares were **49.13% for governor, 45.84% for Senate, and 46.46% for CD5 House**. Corresponding margin changes were **+29.1, +22.6 and +23.8 points**. The Democratic governor candidate ran ahead of the Democratic Senate candidate within the same geography. This is evidence that office/candidate context matters; it does not identify why individual voters made their choices.

These are **matched-unit estimates, not the complete election totals**. Comparable units account for 91.3% of downloaded geographic governor/Senate vote volume and 91.6% of geographic CD5 House vote volume. Administrative ballots are excluded from these comparisons. Full downloaded CD5 House Democratic share, including administrative votes, is 46.81%, versus 46.46% in the matched subset. Coverage and the comparison estimand matter.

## Statewide precinct-context patterns

Q1 and Q4 below mean the lowest and highest demographic-composition quartiles of comparable governor reporting units, each counted equally when setting thresholds. Bar/statistic values pool actual votes, so larger precincts contribute more to the electoral result. The same statewide thresholds apply across offices and to CD5. These are **not quartiles of people or voters**. All numbers below are changes in D–R margin versus 2024 president, in percentage points.

| Context dimension | Governor, Q1 → Q4 | Senate, Q1 → Q4 | Shape across all four groups |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Non-Hispanic Black adult share, 2020 | +20.5 → +17.4 | +13.6 → +14.7 | Peaks in Q3: +27.8 / +22.4 |
| Non-Hispanic White adult share, 2020 | +17.9 → +19.4 | +15.1 → +12.2 | Peaks in Q2: +28.3 / +22.6 |
| Hispanic adult share, ACS 2020–24 | +25.0 → +28.7 | +20.2 → +23.0 | Increases across all four quartiles |
| Adults 18–34 as share of adults | +23.9 → +29.3 | +17.8 → +24.2 | Increases across all four quartiles |
| Adults 65+ as share of adults | +29.5 → +23.3 | +24.0 → +17.6 | Decreases across all four quartiles |
| BA+ share among adults 25+ | +26.3 → +27.3 | +22.1 → +20.7 | Broad movement; Q3 largest, not a monotonic college gradient |
| Households below $50,000 | +27.4 → +22.7 | +20.7 → +19.1 | Q3 largest: +28.1 / +23.3 |
| Adult poverty rate | +27.1 → +25.1 | +20.5 → +21.1 | Q3 largest: +27.8 / +23.1 |

The clearest statewide ordered associations are **larger changes in places with younger adult populations, smaller changes in places with older adult populations, and larger changes in places with higher Hispanic adult shares**. Those statements concern places. The highest Hispanic-share quartile begins around only 4.4% Hispanic adults; it is not a set of majority-Hispanic precincts.

Race, income, poverty and education do **not** support a simple “more of this characteristic means more movement” story. For example, the highest Black-adult-share quartile already had a Democratic D–R margin of **+47.8 in 2024**, rising to **+65.1 for governor**. The third quartile moved from **R+30.3 to R+2.4**. Their different starting positions are visible; their individual voter behavior is not. A smaller swing can accompany much stronger Democratic support. Nor does a positive swing necessarily mean a Democratic win: the lowest-Black-share quartile remained **R+55.6** for governor after moving 20.5 points toward Democrats.

## CD5: movement was broad, and the education result is not the expected simple gradient

These results use actual CD5 whole reporting units, rather than every precinct in the six-county study region. The latter extends beyond CD5.

| Context dimension | Governor Q1 → Q4 | Senate Q1 → Q4 | CD5 House Q1 → Q4 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Non-Hispanic Black adult share | +24.1 → +16.9 | +16.3 → +14.4 | +19.0 → +14.2 |
| Non-Hispanic White adult share | +21.5 → +22.5 | +18.1 → +14.6 | +18.2 → +17.0 |
| Hispanic adult share | +22.0 → +28.5 | +15.5 → +22.6 | +16.4 → +23.2 |
| Adults 18–34 | +27.1 → +27.6 | +20.0 → +22.4 | +22.0 → +22.9 |
| Adults 65+ | +28.8 → +26.3 | +23.2 → +18.7 | +23.5 → +21.3 |
| BA+ among adults 25+ | +33.7 → +27.6 | +28.5 → +20.7 | +29.3 → +22.0 |
| Households below $50,000 | +28.5 → +27.6 | +21.6 → +23.7 | +23.0 → +23.9 |
| Adult poverty rate | +27.9 → +28.8 | +21.1 → +24.5 | +22.3 → +24.9 |

Three features deserve emphasis:

- **The lowest-college group has the largest change for all three offices.** Its 29 units, with approximately 6.2–12.5% of adults 25+ holding a BA+, moved +33.7 for governor, +28.5 for Senate and +29.3 for House. The highest-college group contains 86 units, with approximately 25.2–79.4% BA+, and moved +27.6, +20.7 and +22.0. Middle groups are not strictly ordered. This is a result about precincts; it does not establish that adults without degrees switched their votes more often.
- **Age and income show local variation.** The young-adult Q3 group has the largest change for all offices (+30.0 governor, +23.2 Senate, +24.3 House); Q4 is not the peak. The household-income Q3 group also has the largest change for all three offices (+30.4, +24.8, +25.9). Adult-poverty Q2 is the largest (+31.6, +25.0, +26.7). A single rich-versus-poor or young-versus-old explanation would miss these nonmonotonic results.
- **The racial-context patterns resemble the statewide shape.** Black-adult-share Q3 shows the largest change for all three offices (+28.6, +22.8, +23.1); Q4 shows smaller changes. White-adult-share Q2 is the largest for each office. Hispanic-adult-share changes rise across the four groups for all three offices. These dimensions overlap geographically and with age, income and education.

For Jackson County's 30 matched units, Democratic shares were **13.72% in the 2024 presidential race**, **26.14% for governor**, **22.34% for Senate**, and **23.00% for House**. Margin changes were **+24.8, +17.2 and +18.6 points**. Many Jackson quartiles contain fewer than five units and are withheld from the plotted comparisons; countywide matched totals are more stable summaries than those tiny strata. These are vote shares, not estimates of the percentage of residents who voted.

## Population context that accompanies the election pattern

The [2020–24 ACS](https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5.html) describes Alabama as **63.4% non-Hispanic White, 25.6% non-Hispanic Black, and 5.6% Hispanic**; CD5 is **68.2%, 17.5%, and 7.0%**, respectively. These selected population categories are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive. Madison's non-Hispanic Black population share is 23.6%, compared with Jackson's 3.1%; Morgan's Hispanic population share is 10.6%. Population composition differs from adult composition, citizenship, registration and actual participation.

Among resident adults, CD5 is **28.4% ages 18–34 and 21.4% ages 65+**, versus Alabama's **28.8% and 22.9%**. Jackson is older on this measure: 24.0% young adults and 26.4% age 65+. Lauderdale combines a sizable young-adult share (30.2%) with a sizable older share (25.4%). Madison's BA+ share among adults 25+ is **46.4%**, compared with **30.2% Limestone, 29.8% Lauderdale, 23.3% Morgan, 15.9% Jackson and 15.2% Lawrence**. CD5 is 36.1%; Alabama is 28.4%.

Published median household income in 2024 dollars is **$77,752 ±1,731 in CD5** and **$63,999 ±399 statewide**, with 90% sampling MOEs. County medians range from **$51,908 ±1,987 in Jackson** to **$86,499 ±1,491 in Madison**; Limestone is **$83,629 ±4,065**. Households below $50,000 constitute 40.0% statewide, 32.5% in CD5, 48.0% in Jackson and 27.9% in Limestone. Adult poverty rates are 14.0% statewide and 10.5% in CD5. Those are household/adult population measures, not the incomes or poverty status of actual voters.

Housing and employment provide further context: 6.6% of Limestone housing and 5.2% of Madison housing was built in 2020 or later in the ACS period, versus 2.3% statewide. Work from home accounts for 15.1% of Madison workers age 16+, 12.0% in CD5 and 8.8% statewide. These are useful descriptions of settlement/economic differences; the analysis does not estimate their independent political effects.

[Census Vintage 2025 population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/datasets/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html) show growth from the revised April 2020 base to July 2025 of **18.7% in Limestone, 11.7% in Madison, 3.8% in Lauderdale, 3.3% in Jackson, 2.5% in Morgan and 2.3% in Lawrence**. Growth is uneven; it is not evidence that new residents voted in a particular way. The 2020 urban population share ranges from 82.9% in Madison to approximately 0.006% in Lawrence; the latter is a very small actual urban-classified population, not a missing value. [Census 2020 urban/rural definitions and counts](https://api.census.gov/data/2020/dec/dhc/groups/P2.html).

The [latest 2025 ACS one-year release](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/news/data-releases/2025/release-schedule.html), released October 29, 2026, gives a separate benchmark: median household income **$82,099 ±2,987 for CD5** and **$67,663 ±1,147 statewide**, in **2025 dollars**. Madison is $90,428 ±5,239; Limestone is $89,736 ±11,170. Jackson and Lawrence lack these detailed one-year tables because of the population threshold. These figures are not blended into the common small-area ACS baseline; differences from 2020–24 estimates are not clean one-year changes. The 2025 five-year release remains TBD in the verified schedule.

## What remains uncertain

Precinct ACS values are tract estimates allocated using 2020 block adult population, with demographic composition assumed uniform within each tract. Original 90% sampling MOEs are retained in the underlying demographic tables; they omit allocation and precinct-crosswalk uncertainty. No ratio MOE or electoral-effect confidence interval is claimed. Race, age, income, education, geography and candidates covary; separate quartile charts do not isolate independent effects. Different participation, preferences, residential change, office/candidate differences, and coverage can all contribute to an aggregate shift. The data cannot separate those mechanisms or establish individual vote switching.

The correct statement is **“places with this demographic profile showed this electoral change.”** It is not a measurement of a demographic group's vote, turnout, or causal contribution.

# Completeness report · revised November 17, 2026

The revised atlas retains **49 contested candidate-race scopes and 9 ballot questions** and removes **58 uncontested scopes**. State Board of Education 8 is shown as three requested county portions of one multicounty race; those are not separate district-wide elections. All seven congressional races and every contested House/Senate race touching the six focus counties remain. Uncontested Jackson House 22/23 are removed as requested.

## Results and crosswalk audit

Independent extraction of the original 67 XLS workbooks found **zero normalization differences** across 300,789 numeric cells. All source candidate sums reconcile. All original 2024 presidential baseline counts and mapped baseline sums also reconcile independently. 60,419 blank source cells remain blank; no partial candidate-choice tables were found. 865 statewide ballot-accounting discrepancies remain unresolved rather than repaired.

The precinct layer starts with the 2026 statewide file constructed for the earlier primary project: `outputs/alabama-2026-legislative-district-primary-turnout/data/precincts/AL_precincts.gpkg`. The accidentally downloaded 2026 CCD archive is excluded. Madison now uses its official 79-feature 2026 county GIS layer, matched uniquely to the source names and independently checked against the same-election provider map. Every updated full-precision polygon was rechecked against the 2024 baseline. At least 99% mutual area continuity, complete historical returns, no reuse of old precincts, and matching district electorates are required for an observed whole-unit shift. Split House/Senate rows with exactly one continuous historical precinct use that precinct’s 2024 margin as an explicitly estimated benchmark. This assumes a uniform historical margin within the precinct; exact historical district-fragment returns are unavailable. Neither year’s vote counts are allocated or changed. # Alabama May primary turnout among registered voters

[Map PNG](alabama-2026-primary-turnout-registered-voters.png) · [Map SVG](alabama-2026-primary-turnout-registered-voters.svg) · [Precinct data](precinct-turnout.csv) · [VAP-band table](turnout-by-black-vap-band.csv)

May 19, 2026 precinct primary ballots divided by registered voters. Includes
nonpartisan ballots. Absentee/provisional reporting categories are preserved in
source/county audits but cannot be placed in residential precincts and are excluded
from map fills and demographic buckets. These mapped rates therefore exclude
those voters; they are not complete turnout including absentee voting.

Registration is reported in 1,085 precincts
and **estimated in 838 precincts** across
36 counties, as authorized by the user.
Zero placeholders and incomplete consolidated precinct denominators are treated
as missing. Usable reported precinct counts are preserved. The remaining May
county active+inactive registered-voter total is allocated among missing
precincts proportional to 2020 Census VAP, with registration bounded below by
observed ballots. A zero-VAP prior uses a 1e-6 floor only for numerical feasibility.
Fully observed counties retain their primary-workbook counts; their differences
from monthly May totals are recorded in `registration-estimation-audit.csv`.
Estimated counts are fractional; full precision is used in rates, rounded counts
are shown on the image. Migration and actual registration patterns can differ.

Rates are ratios of sums, never unweighted averages of precinct percentages.
`Est. reg.` counts precincts with estimated denominators. Observed-only rates and
coverage checks remain recoverable from the precinct CSV. This table describes
precinct composition, not individual racial turnout.

African American VAP means 2020 Census Black-alone adults age 18+, including
Hispanic ethnicity (PL P4). Census counts from all 1,947 source precincts are
consolidated once to 1,923 reporting units using the existing complete crosswalk.
Bands are [0,20), [20,40), [40,60), [60,80), [80,100], in percentage points.
Zero-VAP precincts lack a VAP band. All counts and excluded categories remain in
the CSVs. Estimated-registration counts are available in its CSV.

[Comparison CSV](electorate-comparison-by-black-vap-band.csv)

# 2026 Alabama U.S. Senate primary precinct results

This directory contains the first statewide precinct-level reconciliation for
the May 19, 2026 Democratic and Republican U.S. Senate primaries.

## Current coverage

| Party | Matched 2024 polygons | Total polygons | Unresolved source/geometry records |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Democratic | 1,925 | 1,978 | 53 |
| Republican | 1,925 | 1,978 | 53 |

Every 2026 polling-place return is now assigned. The 53 unresolved records are

## Matching method

1. Reuse verified polling-place aliases, relocations, nearest-former-location
   assignments, and aggregation rules developed for Alabama CD-5.
2. Match exact and high-confidence normalized polling-place labels within each
   county.

   variants.
5. Merge Jefferson 3010/3015 for the May 19 temporary combined voting site.
6. Use official county change notices, polling lists, and precinct maps to
   identify splits, relocations, and renamed facilities.
7. Geocode current physical addresses and assign them to the containing 2024
   polygon; sum multiple current returns when they land in the same old polygon.
8. Apply one shared crosswalk to both party contests.
9. Assign the remaining renamed 2026 locations to their nearest reasonable old
   polygon, preferring a nearby empty polygon over an unrelated dual allocation.

# Alabama historical electorate composition

[Figure PNG](alabama-2017-2018-2024-2026-electorate-composition.png) · [Figure SVG](alabama-2017-2018-2024-2026-electorate-composition.svg) · [Comparison CSV](four-election-comparison.csv)

Same 1,923 reporting units and fixed 2020 Census Black-alone VAP bands as the
[2024/May 2026 comparison](../alabama-2026-primary-registered-turnout/README.md).
The measure is each band's share of geographically reported total ballots.
The 2018 election is the November general election containing the governor race;
total ballots, including contest undervotes, are used consistently with 2024/2026.
No registration estimates enter this calculation. These are precinct-composition
shares, not individual racial vote shares or reconstructed historical VAP.

## Historical placement is estimated

2017/2018 VEST precinct candidate returns include allocated county absentee votes.
Provider documentation: [2017](https://election.lab.ufl.edu/data-downloads/resultsdata/2017/precinct/documentation.txt),
[2018](https://election.lab.ufl.edu/data-downloads/resultsdata/2018/precinct/documentation.txt).
For candidate c in county k, multiply each published precinct count by
official geographic candidate votes / official all-category candidate votes.
This reverses the documented proportional allocation approximately, allowing for
integer rounding and provider corrections to defective raw returns. Next scale
the summed candidate distribution to that county's official geographic total
ballots, including contest undervotes. County totals are exact; precinct placement
is a model. A zero raw candidate count uses the county's geographic ballot fraction
and is flagged in the county audit. The raw workbooks and provider documentation
are preserved with hashes; corrected VEST totals are not claimed to be certified
ballot totals. The provider documents candidate-return corrections in eight
counties per year, making the absentee reversal approximate there.

Historical precincts are allocated to 2024 units using 2020 block-VAP weights,
then consolidated to the current reporting units. The existing 2017 crosswalk is
reused; the 2018 crosswalk is cached with input/code hashes. Weights preserve each
source precinct and county total. Any nearest block assignments, geometry repairs
and zero-VAP area fallbacks are recorded in `audit.json`.

`historical-scope-sensitivity.csv` repeats the analysis using pooled candidate
distributions before candidate-specific absentee adjustment, while retaining the
same county geographic totals. This is a method sensitivity, not an uncertainty
interval. The main historical estimates are marked with asterisks in the figure.

| Black VAP | 2017 Senate* | 2018 governor* | 2024 | May 2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0–<20% | 55.64% | 58.08% | 62.43% | 56.02% |
| 20–<40% | 19.91% | 20.16% | 20.00% | 20.19% |
| 40–<60% | 8.48% | 8.02% | 6.88% | 8.17% |
| 60–<80% | 8.07% | 7.17% | 5.83% | 8.07% |

collections.notes:
README.md

# Southern Midterm Counterfactual

![Five-state hypothetical precinct results](alabama-mississippi-midterm-scenario.png)

An illustrative 2026 midterm scenario on 2024 precinct geography, covering
Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina. Mississippi is
calibrated to D+0.5, with Black Democratic support anchored to Presley's estimated
96% in 2023. Identical party-retention and within-race persuasion rates apply
across all five states.

| State | Modeled margin | Turnout as % of 2024 | Turnout share of margin swing |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Louisiana | D+0.7 | 77.1% | 34.3% |
| Mississippi | D+0.5 | 77.1% | 33.3% |
| Alabama | R+8.9 | 76.6% | 34.5% |
| Georgia | D+18.4 | 78.4% | 39.6% |
| South Carolina | D+2.2 | 77.4% | 39.4% |

**The image's “Turnout (% of 2024)” columns are retention percentages:** the
number of modeled returning voters divided by that same group's 2024 two-party
voters. They are not turnout among eligible or registered people, or absolute
vote counts. For example, 82.8 means 82.8 modeled voters return for every 100
voters in that group's 2024 baseline.

The figure retains the white-paper editorial style, thin precinct lines and
five-point blue/red margin bands. A single large regional
map occupies most of the graphic, with large party-colored statewide margins
above each state and modeled demographic turnout/vote splits in a compact table
beneath it. The footer credits Instagram `@topsoilintraining`, X `@electionsjack`
and [Jackson Hannan on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jackson-hannan/),
with clickable profile links in SVG. The existing
bundle path is retained for continuity; the title and scope now cover five states.

## Model

Hold Democratic participation at 85% of the 2024 Democratic baseline. In
Mississippi, first allocate one-third of the required margin shift to turnout,
then two-thirds to persuasion. If p is the certified 2024 Democratic two-party
share and t=0.5025, set the turnout-only share to q=p+(t-p)/3 and solve
b=0.85*D*(1-q)/(q*R). Republican retention is **72.1596%**.

Fit Black Republican-to-Democratic crossover to Mississippi Black D96%, and fit
non-Black crossover to Mississippi statewide D50.25%. The resulting fractions
of returning 2024 Republican voters switching Democratic are **73.2726% for
Black voters** and **7.8362% for non-Black voters**. This is a race-dependent
change in a small baseline Republican group, not a 73-point swing of all Black
voters.

For each estimated racial cell, with x its relevant crossover rate:

    modeled_D = 0.85 * baseline_D + x * b * baseline_R
    modeled_R = (1-x) * b * baseline_R
    margin_pp = 100 * (modeled_D - modeled_R) / (modeled_D + modeled_R)

Sum cells to precincts and states. Both parties' turnout falls; Republican
participation falls more. Turnout acts before persuasion. Exactly one-third of
Mississippi's swing is turnout; the other states' shares differ because their
baseline coalitions differ, as reported above. Common within-group changes are
preserved rather than fitting a different turnout model separately in each state.
The original Alabama and Mississippi numerical results are unchanged.

The 96% target comes from [Split Ticket's November 27, 2023
analysis](https://split-ticket.org/2023/11/27/what-happened-in-mississippi/).
It is a modeled estimate, not a certified racial ballot count. Only this Black
support anchor is transferred from 2023; Presley's overall result and White
support are not constraints.

## Sources and geographic allocation

The supplied RDH archives are preserved unchanged:

- `alabama/data/geospatial/election-precincts/al-2024-gen-prec.zip`
- `mississippi/ms_2024_gen_prec.zip`
- `louisiana/la_2024_gen_prec.zip`
- `georgia/ga_2024_gen_prec.zip`
- `south carolina/sc_2024_gen_prec.zip`

Read the original archives' `*_2024_gen_all_prec` layers. This yields 12,370
unique precinct records: LA 3,656; MS 1,735; AL 1,947; GA 2,720; SC 2,312.
Source README files, source hashes and software versions are in the provenance.
Non-geographic ballots are allocated by the source provider as documented in
those READMEs; Louisiana's parish-level absentee/provisional ballots, for example,
are allocated to precincts by candidate-specific precinct shares within each parish.

Candidate totals are checked against the local [FEC certified 2024 presidential
results](https://www.fec.gov/documents/5645/2024presgeresults.xlsx).
Louisiana, Georgia, South Carolina and Alabama match exactly. Mississippi's raw
Harris total is one below certification; preserve raw counts and proportionally
calibrate derived Democratic weights. No source returns are overwritten.

Georgia has 18 source precinct records with COUNTYFP `000`: three in Chattahoochee
and fifteen in Fulton. Restore those codes only from unambiguous county-name/code
pairs in that same source archive. Preserve original codes in
`source_county_fips`, resolved codes in `county_fips` and the repair count in
`model-audit.json`. No precinct geometry or vote count is changed by this repair.

The racial geographic proxy is 2020 Census P3_004N Black-alone adults divided by
P3_001N total adults. Official PL files are retained for
[Alabama](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Alabama/al2020.pl.zip),
[Mississippi](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Mississippi/ms2020.pl.zip),
[Louisiana](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Louisiana/la2020.pl.zip),
[Georgia](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Georgia/ga2020.pl.zip) and
[South Carolina](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/South_Carolina/sc2020.pl.zip).

All 558,518 positive-adult-population blocks are assigned uniquely within their
source counties. Mississippi uses the supplied RDH block-to-precinct IDs; the
other states use Census block internal points within precinct polygons. No
nearest assignment was needed. County/state Census adult and Black-adult totals
reconcile. For precincts with zero assigned adult population, use the county
adult-race fraction: eight Louisiana precincts, nineteen Georgia and two South
Carolina. These are audited proxy fallbacks, not observed voter demographics.

Within each state and 2024 party, calibrate the Black fraction of precinct ballots
with a bounded common log-odds adjustment to the geographic proxy, clipped to
[1e-6,1-1e-6]. Match the state's published 2024 survey Black electorate share and
normalized Black D/R preferences, while preserving every precinct's observed
party totals and keeping racial weights within each party's ballot total.
Apply the common race-specific persuasion rates to these cells. Thus racial
calibration affects the map and table coherently. It does not identify individual
voters' race or choices.

## Demographic table

Published 2024 Fox News Voter Analysis, conducted by NORC, supplies electorate
shares and Harris/Trump preferences:
[Alabama](https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2024/general-results/state/alabama),
[Mississippi](https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2024/general-results/state/mississippi),
[Louisiana](https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2024/general-results/state/louisiana),
[Georgia](https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2024/general-results/state/georgia) and
[South Carolina](https://www.foxnews.com/elections/2024/general-results/state/south-carolina).
HTML snapshots and exact selected source rows/hashes are retained locally and
in `demographic-inputs.json`.

Normalize the source's Harris/Trump shares to a two-party denominator. Do not
interpret suppressed 0/0 preferences as zero support. Rounded complete education
partitions are calibrated with a shared log-odds offset to preserve their odds
ratio while matching statewide or White-voter baseline preferences. Preserve the
original survey percentages separately from adjusted model inputs.

Build six race/education cells per state: White, Black and Other, each No BA/BA+.
White education uses the survey's observed White education shares/preferences;
overall education uses calibrated survey margins. Subtract White cells to obtain
the non-White residual by education and baseline party. Allocate this residual
between Black and Other, assuming equal education composition conditional on
baseline party. This unobserved association is an explicit assumption. Other-race
support is a residual and is not displayed as a reported survey estimate.

Apply the same Black/non-Black crossover and party-retention parameters to all
cells. The 30 modeled cells reconcile to all 30 displayed group/state rows,
statewide results and precinct racial totals. Race, education and White education
are overlapping tabulations; they must not be added together. BA+ means a
bachelor's degree or more; No BA includes some college and associate degrees.
Unrounded cells and group results accompany the figure in audit CSVs.

## Display and limitations

Projection: EPSG:5070. Invalid projected polygons are repaired only when needed
with Shapely's structure method and no snapping; repair counts/area changes are
audited. Full precinct geometry is retained. Independent [Census county
boundaries](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2025/shp/cb_2025_us_county_500k.zip)
provide the 418 county/parish borders and state outlines. Merge contiguous county
line segments before 150-metre display simplification on the regional map. The regional tolerance is below one output pixel and
does not change precinct geometry, returns, racial proxies or modeled results.

Use stroke-free fills plus a separate thin dark precinct boundary overlay.
Blue means a Democratic lead, red Republican. Directional bin lower bounds are
0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55 and 60 percentage points; 60+ is the
upper open-ended band. Ties are cream; gray means no baseline two-party votes.
Missing margins remain missing. PNG/SVG have a common palette and class breaks.

The opaque PNG is 3,600×3,300 at 300 dpi. SVG retains vector text and administrative
outlines with embedded 300-dpi precinct fills/lines. SVG path coordinates are
rounded to 0.001 point, less than 0.003 raster pixel, to reduce file size; image
and text content remain unchanged. Alt text and classification
metadata are in `map_spec.json`.

These are hypothetical generic-party results, not candidate forecasts. No new
voters, minor parties or uncertainty intervals are modeled. Census adult race
is an ecological proxy; Census and survey racial categories differ. Survey
percentages are rounded, subgroup samples are limited and the residual joint
race/education allocation is not identified by the published margins. Income
is not independently estimated. Common within-group rates cannot capture all
local or candidate differences. Matched demographic swings alone would not
identify a unique state or precinct result without these explicit assumptions.

This map was created using data from the Redistricting Data Hub.
[RDH terms and conditions](https://redistrictingdatahub.org/terms-and-conditions/).

## Rebuild and verify

```bash
uv run python scripts/create-alabama-mississippi-midterm-scenario-map.py
uv run pytest -q tests/test_alabama_mississippi_midterm.py tests/test_alabama_2026_governor_rendering.py tests/test_cartography.py tests/test_output_contract.py
uv run election-maps validate-outputs outputs/alabama-mississippi-2026-midterm-scenario
```

The rebuild writes `mississippi/data/alabama-midterm-comparison/five-state-precinct-scenario.gpkg`.
The earlier two-state output is checkpointed under the same local data directory
in `before-five-state-expansion/`. Original archives stay unchanged. No commit,
push, deployment or external publication is performed.
