# Cook essay comparison charts

Use the first three graphics as the essay sequence. The fourth is a useful
supporting figure. [View all four together](images/compare-all-four.png) or
[open the four-page PDF](compare-all-four.pdf).

| Graphic | Purpose | Why this form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [01 · Higher vote retention in Black areas](images/01-contest-vote-retention.png) | Compare retention directly: 87.7% versus 76.9%. | Aligned dots show the difference without requiring a matrix lookup; intervals expose uncertainty. |
| [02 · Democratic gains by age profile](images/02-democratic-gains-by-age.png) | Compare both age patterns on one scale. | A two-series profile shows the larger White-area gradient and nearly flat Black-area pattern together. |
| [03 · Young White vs. younger Black areas](images/03-young-white-vs-younger-black.png) | Compare White areas at 30–<40% young adults with Black areas at 40–100%. | A direct comparison isolates the cross-age question; the Black comparison areas are strictly younger by the measured population share. |
| [04 · Vote retention within states](images/04-retention-within-states.png) | Check the pooled retention result against state composition. | Common-scale state rows reveal missing or weak coverage instead of implying every state contributes equally. |

The paired-dot charts use the same visual grammar. The age profile combines two
questions in one graphic. Together these are easier to compare than a large
race-by-age heatmap, and they preserve the magnitudes rather than translating
them into color intensity alone.

## What the data says

These are precinct-area comparisons, not individual-voter findings.

| Comparison | Point difference | 95% county-resampling interval | Interpretation within this selected sample |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Black minus White vote retention | +10.8 pp | +7.4 to +12.7 pp | A clear retention difference. It is not a race-specific turnout rate. |
| Younger minus older Black-area Democratic share gain | +0.7 pp | −2.5 to +1.6 pp | A small descriptive difference; the age claim remains uncertain. |
| Younger minus older White-area Democratic share gain | +2.7 pp | +0.8 to +5.2 pp | A larger gain in the highest-young-adult-share band. |
| Young White minus even-younger Black-area Democratic share gain | +5.0 pp | +3.9 to +6.8 pp | White areas at 30–<40% young adults gained more than Black areas at 40–100%. |

Do not write that this set establishes all four proposed claims. In particular,
it does not establish individual Black turnout exceeding individual White
turnout, and the Black-area age contrast is weak. Suggested captions are in
[CAPTIONS.md](CAPTIONS.md).

## Definitions and coverage

- The source panel contains 7,189 matched precincts in Arkansas (1,058), Georgia
  (1,853), South Carolina (2,239), Tennessee (18), and Virginia (2,021), after
  excluding Texas and Florida. It is selected coverage, not a representative
  sample of all Southern precincts or every precinct in these states.
- Black areas have at least 80% Black-alone adult residents; White areas have at
  least 80% non-Hispanic White adult residents. Those are different Census race
  definitions and are kept explicit here. The disjoint cohorts contain 170 and
  2,006 precincts respectively; other precincts remain in the underlying panel
  but are outside these two comparison cohorts.
- Age means the **share of all adult residents aged 18–34**, not the age of
  actual voters or specifically of Black/White voters. The common age bands are
  0–<20%, 20–<30%, 30–<40%, and 40–100%. The age-profile positions are categorical
  and equally spaced, not a fitted continuous age relationship. “Younger” and
  “older” refer to area composition, not individual cohorts.
- Retention is `100 × pooled 2026 D+R Senate votes / pooled 2024 D+R presidential
  votes`. It is not turnout as a share of eligible residents. It can also reflect
  contest participation and candidate differences between elections.
- Democratic gain is the precinct's 2026-minus-2024 **two-party Democratic vote
  share**, averaged using 2024 D+R votes as weights. It is in percentage points,
  not Democratic-versus-Republican margin points; for two-party results, margin
  change would be twice share change. It is not the change in the pooled vote
  share of a group with shifting precinct weights.
- † means fewer than 30 precincts, fewer than three county clusters, or fewer
  than 5,000 baseline votes. Black age-band endpoints contain 11 and 18
  precincts. Arkansas has only two qualifying Black-area precincts in two
  counties. Tennessee has no qualifying Black areas and only 17 qualifying
  White-area precincts in one county. No interval is drawn below three counties.

## Uncertainty and sensitivity

The 2,500-draw bootstrap resamples whole county clusters within each state, with
replacement, retaining each state's original number of county draws. All
precincts in a county receive the same multiplicity. The same draws are used
for both sides of each contrast, preserving their covariance. Seed: 20261112.
Intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of finite draws. Eighteen draws
contain no eligible older Black-area precinct, leaving 2,482 valid Black-age
contrast draws; these are reported rather than replaced with zero.

This is exploratory analysis: the means were inspected before the resampling
plan. The intervals describe stability within the selected panel and do not
measure population representativeness, causal identification, Census composition
error, or changes in candidate appeal. No p-values or confirmatory claims are
made. The state chart is a coverage check, not a state-adjusted estimate.

The primary 80% race-area definition remains fixed. The accompanying
[threshold sensitivity table](data/threshold-sensitivity.csv) also reports 50%
and 60% definitions without selecting a more favorable result. The Black age
contrast spans zero at all three thresholds. Small-cell observations are retained.

## Design and exports

All four use the established Cook frame: logo on the left, Merriweather Bold
headlines, Open Sans labels, navy rules, named-state sources, and the three social
profiles. Black areas use navy circles; White areas use slate squares and a
dashed profile line. Marker shape and direct labels distinguish series without
relying on color. Cook red remains in the logo so it does not imply a Republican
series. Titles, labels, definitions, and sources carry information; no generic
essay banners or promotional subtitles have been added.

- `images/`: opaque 3900 × 3600 PNGs at 600 dpi, plus a 2 × 2 overview.
- `pdf/`: one-page vector PDFs at 6.5 × 6 inches, with embedded fonts.
- `svg/`: portable SVGs with embedded font subsets.
- `compare-all-four.pdf`: four-page review copy.
- Insert individual PNGs or SVGs at **6.5 inches wide** in Word; use the PDFs for
  vector placement in a PDF layout. Avoid scaling wider than the text column.
- Font and icon provenance/licenses are retained alongside the copied assets.
  The Cook logo is reused from the established reference set; the graphics are
  application work samples, not claims of publication by Cook.

## Reproduction and audit

From the Election-Maps repository:

```sh
.venv/bin/python outputs/cook-essay-comparison-charts-2026-11-12/analyze.py
.venv/bin/python outputs/cook-essay-comparison-charts-2026-11-12/render.py
.venv/bin/python outputs/cook-essay-comparison-charts-2026-11-12/verify.py
```

`analyze.py` reads the original matched panel without modifying it. `render.py`
reuses the existing Cook renderer and assets. `verify.py` independently rebuilds
cohort membership, point estimates, all county-resampling replicates, and
intervals from raw rows; it checks plotted labels, export metadata, embedded
fonts, source credits, and preservation hashes for earlier inputs/artifacts.
Evidence is in `analysis.json`, `provenance.json`, `verification.json`, and
`visual-review.json`. Complete group membership and resampling draws are in
`data/`. No prior charts or raw inputs are overwritten.

# Florida Special Election Results and Swing

Observed swing from the November 2024 presidential election to the March 24, 2026 special elections in precincts where Hispanic/Latino adults exceed 50% of 2020 Census voting-age population. The same precinct set is used in both elections.

| District | Latino-majority precincts | 2024 margin | 2026 margin | Swing toward Democrats |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SD14 | 27 | R+8.5 | D+4.4 | +12.9 pp |
| HD51 | 3 | D+0.9 | D+20.4 | +19.5 pp |
| HD87 | 3 | R+6.3 | D+18.2 | +24.5 pp |

## Calculation

Select precincts with positive Census adult population and `Hispanic/Latino VAP > total VAP / 2`; exactly 50% does not qualify. Sum Democratic and Republican votes separately across the selected precincts in each election. Margin = `100 × (D − R) / (D + R)`; swing = special-election margin minus presidential margin. Precinct margins are not averaged. These are observed neighborhood results, including all voters in the selected precincts; they do not isolate Latino individuals or distinguish persuasion from turnout changes. No ecological vote-choice model is used.

[Selected precincts and vote counts](latino-majority-precincts.csv) · [Pooled totals and calculations](latino-majority-summary.csv)

## Geography and sources

2020 Census PL 94-171 P4 provides Hispanic/Latino adults of any race (P4_002N) and total adults (P4_001N). Census block internal points in NAD83 (EPSG:4269) are transformed to EPSG:5070 and assigned to 2024 precinct geometry using `within`. The demographic classification stays fixed across elections; population changes after 2020 are not measured.

The 2024 baseline is the downloaded RDH precinct archive, fields G24PREDHAR and G24PRERTRU. Its README discloses proportional county-vote allocations in Hillsborough and Palm Beach. March 2026 official candidate returns match state totals exactly. Cross-year matching uses county code and precinct ID; identical IDs do not prove unchanged boundaries. Precinct geometry is clipped to 2024 Census legislative districts. One non-majority HD51 precinct has a population split, so its overall-district baseline is allocated by Census VAP; all 33 selected majority precincts retain their full 2024 votes.

All 152 SD14 and 37 HD51 IDs match; 154 of 156 HD87 IDs match. HD87 precincts 3507 (17 candidate votes) and 8490 (1) lack 2024 IDs. They remain in official totals and outside the mapped comparison. Current county polygons for both contain zero 2020 adult population, so they cannot qualify as Latino-majority under the stated definition. The separate crosswalk records their spatial predecessors without copying a parent’s baseline votes into multiple successor precincts.

Crosswalk detail: [precinct-crosswalk.csv](precinct-crosswalk.csv), [crosswalk audit](precinct-crosswalk-audit.json), and [source notes](precinct-crosswalk-sources.md). The live county GIS snapshot was edited June 2026; January 2025 official creation maps and February 2026 changes provide supporting context. Spatial overlaps describe the downloaded vintage and are not certified vote-allocation weights. No crosswalk allocation is needed for the selected majority-precinct calculation.

The three-county Census join explicitly audits six positive-population blocks (130 adults) outside the precinct polygons. Unassigned district VAP is 36 adults in SD14, 1 in HD51 and 48 in HD87. These geometric and vintage limitations remain in the coverage audit. No nearest-neighbor population assignment is used. Whole zero-VAP precincts retain observed 2024 votes for overall comparisons but cannot qualify as majority precincts.

[Official results and source verification](sources.md) · [Geographic audit](geography-audit.json)

## Maps and rebuild

Six precinct maps show special-election results and swing from 2024, plus a combined overview, exported as PNG and SVG. Colors use 10-point D/R margin bins, saturated at 60+ points; gray indicates unavailable values, hatching exact ties, and pale blue district area outside archive precinct coverage. On-map summaries now show the direct Latino-majority precinct calculation. Detailed definitions remain here. Prior ecological-model outputs are archived locally under `florida/data/previous-ecological-analysis-2026-11-01/` and are superseded.

```bash
.venv/bin/python scripts/florida_special_returns.py
.venv/bin/python scripts/florida_special_crosswalk.py
.venv/bin/python scripts/create-florida-2026-special-election-maps.py
.venv/bin/election-maps validate-outputs outputs/florida-2026-special-elections
.venv/bin/election-maps gallery
```

Local source staging: downloaded 2024 and 2026 election ZIPs in `florida/`; [Census Florida PL ZIP](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Florida/fl2020.pl.zip) under `florida/data/census-2020/`; [2024 upper](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2024/SLDU/tl_2024_12_sldu.zip) and [lower district ZIPs](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2024/SLDL/tl_2024_12_sldl.zip) under `florida/data/`, extracted into matching stem directories. Crosswalk sources are cached under `florida/data/crosswalk/`.

collections.notes:
README.md

# Kansas presidential swing relative to the nation, 2016–2024

The [precinct map](kansas-2016-2024-relative-partisan-swing.png) shows the change
in Democratic-minus-Republican presidential margin **relative to the national
popular-vote margin**, in percentage points. Blue is leftward, red is rightward.
The [SVG](kansas-2016-2024-relative-partisan-swing.svg) keeps labels and
administrative outlines as vectors, with precinct fills embedded at 300 dpi.
The editorial styling follows the latest Alabama governor polling precinct map:
white background, Nimbus Sans typography, muted red/blue colors, ruled summary
table and four metro windows focused on dense urban precincts.
Kansas uses a landscape layout to accommodate its wider outline.

The windows have local scales: Kansas City (Kansas side) 52 × 41.6 km, Wichita
26 × 20.8 km, Topeka 18 × 14.4 km, and Lawrence 14 × 11.2 km. Each window
prints its dimensions. Their finer, shared precinct edges are drawn once in
muted charcoal, so dense precincts remain legible without accumulating white
polygon strokes.
The Kansas City window includes the northern city riverfront along the Missouri
border while retaining the Kansas City and Johnson County suburbs at metro scale.

## Calculation

For each year, `margin = 100 × (Democratic votes − Republican votes) /
all recorded presidential votes`. Then:

```text
relative lean 2016 = precinct margin 2016 − national margin 2016
relative lean 2024 = precinct margin 2024 − national margin 2024
relative swing = relative lean 2024 − relative lean 2016
```

A positive value is leftward. This is a change in margin, not half the change
in margin and not a percentage change in a vote share. The user's example is
`(1 − (−1.5)) − (−16 − 2.1) = +20.6` percentage points left.

National margins are calculated from unrounded FEC vote counts:

| Year | Democratic votes | Republican votes | All presidential votes | D minus R |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2016 | 65,853,514 | 62,984,828 | 136,669,276 | +2.098998 pp |
| 2024 | 75,017,613 | 77,302,580 | 155,238,302 | −1.471909 pp |

The nation moved 3.570908 points right, so a precinct's relative swing equals
its raw Democratic-minus-Republican margin change **plus 3.570908 points**.
Kansas moved from R+22.54 relative lean to R+14.64, a **7.90-point leftward
relative swing**, using the supplied precinct returns. The statewide figure is
calculated from statewide vote totals, not an unweighted average of precincts.

## Comparable boundaries and missing returns

The archives contain 4,021 source precincts for 2016 and 4,193 for 2024. The map
uses 2024 geography. County FIPS codes are linked from Census county records.
All spatial calculations use CONUS Albers equal-area coordinates, EPSG:5070.

The crosswalk reuses the repository's Tennessee polygon-intersection and
reciprocal-overlap helpers. It transfers a source precinct's complete votes if
at least 99% of its area falls in one 2024 precinct. Reciprocal 99% pairs are
classified as unchanged geometry. This is a near-identical geometry threshold,
not proof that every historical boundary vertex is identical. Whole-source
transfers also accommodate precinct mergers.

For splits, the script assigns 2020 Census block internal points to both
geographies, totals their voting-age population (P3_001N), and allocates each
2016 candidate's votes in proportion to VAP. Each block is assigned once within
its county; boundary/overlap ambiguity is resolved by greatest distance from a
polygon boundary, then stable source row ID. In this dataset **all 104,252
positive-VAP blocks match both geographies without ambiguity or missing VAP**.
No nearest-neighbor joins are used. Area allocation is used only for sources
without assigned positive VAP: 175 source polygons holding just 85 recorded
presidential votes. This fallback is identified in the crosswalk.

Weights sum to one for every 2016 source precinct. Every candidate's votes are
conserved separately within all 105 counties; the maximum reconciliation error
in this build is zero. The split allocation assumes constant candidate support
within each source precinct. It is an estimate, not observed 2016 returns on
2024 boundaries. Zero-return source polygons are not assigned a partisan margin.

There are **3,624 comparable precincts**: 2,489 swing left and 1,135 swing right
relative to the nation. Of these, 1,282 receive some estimated split allocation.
Another **569 polygons are gray**: 447 have no recorded 2024 presidential votes,
and 122 have positive 2024 returns but no positive reconstructed 2016 baseline.
Zero counts can reflect uninhabited geography or reporting arrangements; these
files alone do not establish which explanation applies to every polygon.

Original geometries contained 10 invalid polygons in 2016 and 29 in 2024. These
were repaired with Shapely `make_valid(method="structure", keep_collapsed=False)`;
maximum relative area changes are below 4 × 10⁻¹⁵. No snapping was applied.
Analysis, the local GeoPackage and precinct fills retain full geometry detail.
The display uses stroke-free, non-antialiased polygon fills to prevent white
seams. Precinct polygons are not simplified independently. County/state linework
comes from independent Census 2025 cartographic county boundaries, filtered to
Kansas; it is simplified by 30 metres with topology preservation. It is never
derived from precinct coverage gaps. For example, dissolving the supplied
precincts creates 688 internal rings in Douglas County and 96 in Sedgwick County;
drawing those rings as county borders caused the former black dashes. All 105
Kansas Census reference polygons are valid, contiguous, and hole-free. The county
reference is display context and is not used to reallocate votes. Insets are
clipped to their windows before drawing
unique, thin precinct boundaries. Precinct fills and fine inset linework are
embedded in the SVG at 300 dpi to preserve detail within its file-size limit;
text and administrative context remain vector artwork. This is an export choice
and never changes calculated votes, margins or the geographic source data.
The SVG shares repeated styles through CSS classes and rounds path coordinates
to 0.01 point (maximum rounding error 0.021 pixel at 300 dpi); text and style
values remain intact. This keeps the vector below the repository's 5 MiB limit.

## Source discrepancy

The supplied 2016 Democratic and Republican totals match the FEC exactly, as do
Johnson's and Stein's totals. However, `G16PREOTH` contains **16,750 write-ins**,
while the FEC Kansas table lists **7,467 votes across named write-in candidates**.
Thus, the supplied 2016 total is 1,193,685, versus the FEC's 1,184,402: a difference
of **9,283**. The supplied README does not explain that difference. This map
preserves the supplied precinct denominator; it does not invent a distribution
of the discrepancy across precincts. Using the FEC statewide denominator would
make the statewide relative swing about 0.16 points more Democratic. All 2024
candidate totals and the statewide denominator match the FEC exactly.

## Sources and files

- `kansas/ks_vest_16.zip`: user-supplied VEST/RDH archive. Its README attributes
  returns to OpenElections and boundaries primarily to Census Phase 2 and county
  sources, with local revisions; RDH retrieval date November 7, 2022.
- `kansas/ks_2024_gen_prec.zip`: user-supplied VEST/IKE Lab/RDH archive;
  RDH retrieval date September 12, 2025.
- [FEC 2016 workbook](https://www.fec.gov/documents/1890/federalelections2016.xlsx):
  national Table 1 and Kansas rows in `2016 Pres General Results`.
- [FEC 2024 workbook](https://www.fec.gov/documents/5645/2024presgeresults.xlsx):
  national `Total:` row and Kansas `KS` row.
- [Census Kansas PL 94-171 archive](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Kansas/ks2020.pl.zip):
  geography file for county codes and block internal points, and segment 2 for VAP.
- [Census 2025 county cartographic boundaries, 1:500,000](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2025/shp/cb_2025_us_county_500k.zip):
  Kansas county and state outline context; a copy of the existing local Census
  archive is staged under `kansas/data/census-counties/`.

`precinct-relative-swing-audit.csv` contains every 2024 precinct, each year's
vote totals and margins, relative leans, raw and relative swings, and crosswalk
status. `precinct-crosswalk.csv` identifies source and target precincts, weights,
methods and allocated votes. IDs `KS16-####` and `KS24-####` use zero-based source
record order, tied to archived source hashes; they are local stable IDs, not
official precinct identifiers. `audit.json` records reconciliation and missing
data counts; `provenance.json` records source hashes, CRS and package versions.
`manifest.csv` records checksums for the complete publication bundle.

The accessible data alternative is the precinct audit CSV. Map description:
Kansas is predominantly blue for leftward relative swing, with especially strong
leftward movement in much of suburban Johnson County and parts of Wichita.
Red precincts are interspersed across rural Kansas and some urban cores. Gray
polygons lack a comparable positive-vote baseline. Geography describes aggregate
election change and cannot identify individual voters switching parties.

Some precincts have only a handful of votes. Their margins can change by more
than 100 points even with little absolute vote change; bins above 30 points
saturate at the darkest hue, and unrounded values remain in the audit CSV.
Comparable precincts cover 1,322,557 of 1,327,591 recorded 2024 votes (99.62%).

## Rebuild and verify

From the repository root, retaining both supplied Kansas ZIP files:

```bash
uv run python scripts/create-kansas-2016-2024-relative-partisan-swing-map.py
uv run pytest tests/test_kansas_relative_presidential_swing.py -q
uv run election-maps validate-outputs outputs/kansas-2016-2024-relative-partisan-swing
```

The script extracts expected local shapefile components and fetches public
reference files only when absent. It reuses the project's existing Census county
archive before downloading that reference. Downloaded sources and the full-detail
`kansas/data/kansas-relative-swing.gpkg` remain local. Source hashes support exact
input comparison if a remote file later changes. The renderer imports the
existing Alabama polling renderer and Tennessee crosswalk helpers; those scripts
remain unchanged.

Software guidance acknowledgment: Kassis, T., Agarwal, V., He, Y., Patel, D., &
Brueckner, A. M. (2026). *Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge
for Research Agents*, current arXiv version v2, verified October 29, 2026.
[doi:10.48550/arXiv.2609.00065](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.00065).
The GeoPandas and scientific-visualization skills informed validation and export
practice; they are not election-data sources.

# Madison County’s different coalitions: the 2026 general election

The strongest finding is that **Doug Jones reaches beyond the geographic coalition supporting the other Democratic candidates**. Jones has a higher Democratic two-party share than Everett Wess in every one of Madison’s 79 geographic precincts. Andrew Sneed also does better than Wess countywide, particularly in Republican-leaning precincts. Most local and legislative Democrats run behind both. Marilyn Lands is the exception among the six requested legislative Democrats: Lands narrowly exceeds Wess in the comparable precincts while falling short of Jones.

This is an analysis of **November 3, 2026 preliminary returns**, frozen at official Clarity revision **385074**, published November 3 at **10:20:17 p.m. CST**. The validated collector retrieved these source entities on November 5 at approximately **20:33:57 UTC / 2:33:57 p.m. CST**. All 79 geographic precincts have completion status 4 in this snapshot. That is reporting completion, not certification; provisional administrative rows remain separate and corrections remain possible. Sources: [official Madison results](https://results.enr.clarityelections.com/AL/Madison/127483/web.345435/#/summary), [preserved source provenance](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/provenance.json), [official status snapshot](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/official-status.json).

## Maps and scope

Open the [offline interactive atlas](index.html) to switch races and benchmarks, inspect precincts, and sort the data. The [27-page printable atlas](madison-2026-election-atlas.pdf) contains five overview/comparison sheets and 22 individual race/measure pages. Every individual map is also available as PNG and editable SVG under [maps](maps/).

Coverage includes Governor, U.S. Senate and CD-5 in Madison; HD-10, HD-20, HD-21, HD-25, SD-2 and SD-7; all 12 local candidate contests on Madison’s common ballot; and the local private-sewer-system amendment. Local offices comprise two circuit judges, three district judges, sheriff, tax assessor, tax collector, coroner, license director, school superintendent and school board district 3. Source roster: [official common ballot](https://www.sos.alabama.gov/sites/default/files/sample-ballots/2026/gen/Madison-Sample.pdf), [preserved ballot transcription](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/ballot.json).

**HD-25 and SD-2 totals below cover Madison only.** Both districts extend into Limestone, whose district rows are zero and unreported in the preserved dashboard snapshot. These are not full-district outcomes. CD-5’s figures similarly describe Madison, not its other five counties. HD-10/20/21 and SD-7 have no meaningful outside-Madison county coverage in the prepared district reference. Source: [frozen dashboard coverage](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/dashboard-state.json), [district geography and provenance](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/seat-geography.json).

## The top of the ticket: Jones’s advantage is broad, but uneven

| Madison race | Democratic candidate | D votes | R votes | D share of D/R votes | D vote lead |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Governor | Doug Jones | 92,597 | 66,743 | 58.11% | 25,854 |
| U.S. Senate | Everett Wess | 87,464 | 71,668 | 54.96% | 15,796 |
| CD-5 | Andrew Sneed | 88,667 | 71,028 | 55.52% | 17,639 |

These headline totals include administrative ballots; write-ins are preserved but excluded from the two-party percentage. Jones’s 58.11% two-party share is **57.88% of all Governor votes**, for example. Tables and derived figures throughout this report come from [race-summary.csv](race-summary.csv), [candidate-precinct-votes.csv](candidate-precinct-votes.csv) and [precinct-comparisons.csv](precinct-comparisons.csv), independently reconciled to the [official summary](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/official-summary.json) and [official precinct details](../../alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas/official-details.json).

Jones wins 57 geographic precincts, Sneed 52 and Wess 50. Jones’s advantage over Wess is not confined to a handful of places: it is positive in **all 79**, ranging from approximately **0.12 to 8.31 percentage points of Democratic vote share**. Seven precincts support Jones while giving Wess less than 50%: Cornerstone Presbyterian, Covenant Presbyterian, Weatherly Heights, Aldersgate, Community Fellowship, Locust Grove and Restoration. These are observed precinct outcomes, not an estimate of individual crossover voters. [Precinct comparisons](precinct-comparisons.csv).

**Cornerstone Presbyterian is the most striking example:** Jones takes **52.81%**, Wess **44.50%**, an **8.31-point share difference**. Covenant Presbyterian shows 52.66% versus 46.88%. Jones also improves in places remaining Republican: Southwood Presbyterian gives Jones 42.24%, versus Wess’s 36.38%; Cove Church gives Jones 40.96%, versus Wess’s 35.93%. [Top-ticket map](01-top-ticket.png), [Governor comparison page](maps/governor.png).

To describe coalition differences without guessing voter demographics, I divide precincts into three groups based solely on Wess’s observed Senate share: below 40%, 40–60%, and at least 60%. These are analytical groupings, not racial, class or occupational categories.

| Precinct group, defined by Senate D share | Precincts | Jones vs Wess | Sneed vs Wess |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Below 40% | 17 | +3.76 pp | +1.66 pp |
| 40–60% | 31 | +3.61 pp | +0.59 pp |
| At least 60% | 31 | +2.07 pp | −0.06 pp |

Values average within-precinct share differences using each candidate race’s D/R votes as weights. **Jones’s extra support is largest outside the strongest Democratic precincts; Sneed’s advantage is even more concentrated in the Republican-leaning group.** In the strongest Democratic group, Sneed and Wess perform almost identically. This supports a geographic interpretation of broader reach for Jones and a smaller, distinct reach for Sneed. It does not establish which voters changed parties or why. [Coalition-strata data](coalition-strata.csv), [CD-5 comparison map](maps/cd5.png).

## Legislative races: separate district composition from candidate performance

The first percentage below is the candidate’s observed Madison subtotal, including administrative votes. The two comparison columns use only comparable geographic precincts and therefore describe a narrower electorate. They are **share differences**, not margin differences: a one-point D share change corresponds to a two-point D/R margin change.

| Race | Democratic candidate | Madison D share | D−R vote margin | vs Jones | vs Wess | Comparable precincts | Share of geographic D/R votes covered |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| HD-10 | Marilyn Lands | 60.16% | +4,153 | −2.18 pp | **+0.35 pp** | 5 of 11 | 63.8% |
| HD-20 | James Linderholm | 43.09% | −3,255 | −5.07 pp | −0.94 pp | 8 of 14 | 78.0% |
| HD-21 | Forrest Satterfield | 48.61% | −676 | −5.23 pp | −2.43 pp | 7 of 12 | 69.1% |
| HD-25* | Allison T Montgomery | 53.39% | +1,488 | −4.48 pp | −1.32 pp | 8 of 14 | 76.2% |
| SD-2* | Rudolph Valentino Drake | 56.95% | +7,724 | −6.74 pp | −3.65 pp | 22 of 27 | 87.4% |
| SD-7 | Jared Sluss | 50.48% | +577 | −5.41 pp | −1.88 pp | 30 of 38 | 93.0% |

*Madison portion only; Limestone is unreported. These comparisons do not rank campaign quality: candidate, opponent and local electorate effects are inseparable in these aggregate observations. The excluded split precincts may behave differently. [Legislative overview](02-legislature.png), [summary data](race-summary.csv), [precinct comparisons](precinct-comparisons.csv).

**HD-10: Lands retains an unusually large part of the top-ticket coalition.** Lands exceeds Wess in **all five** unsplit comparison precincts. The largest edge is Town Madison Wellness Center: Lands **63.29%**, Wess **62.55%**, versus Jones **64.66%**. At Triana City Hall, Lands is almost identical to Wess, 75.77% versus 75.75%. The relatively small 0.35-point aggregate edge is consistent across the available clean subset; it should not be extrapolated to the six excluded split precincts. [HD-10 map](maps/hd10.png).

**HD-20: the comparable precincts indicate a substantially less Democratic electorate than in the other requested seats.** On the comparable-precinct measure, Linderholm is only **0.94 points behind Wess**, the second-smallest shortfall after Lands’s positive difference. Monte Sano is almost identical to Wess, 62.33% versus 62.38%; Clubhouse on Green Mountain is **0.83 points ahead**. The larger losses occur at Cove Church and Hampton Cove, **1.95** and **2.18 points behind Wess**. My inference is that district composition explains much of the lower raw Democratic share; this is not an exact decomposition of the full district, because split precincts are excluded. Linderholm’s 43.09% headline share alone would overstate the difference in candidate performance relative to the other legislative Democrats. [HD-20 map](maps/hd20.png).

**HD-21: Reynolds’s advantage is visible even inside precincts supporting other Democrats.** Satterfield trails Wess in **all seven** unsplit precincts. At Optimist Park, Satterfield takes **54.73%**, versus Wess’s **58.49%** and Jones’s **61.06%**. At Chase Park, Satterfield takes **48.33%**, versus Wess’s **50.89%**. These are concrete places where the Republican legislative candidate has a stronger relative result than the Republican Senate candidate. They support a distinct geographic profile for Reynolds without revealing individual ticket splitting. [HD-21 map](maps/hd21.png).

**HD-25: Montgomery leads the Madison subtotal while running below both benchmarks.** Montgomery trails Wess in all eight comparable precincts, with the deficit larger in the competitive Senate group (**−1.54 points**) than in the strongest Democratic group (**−1.01**). At Restoration Church, Montgomery takes **47.73%**, Wess **48.94%** and Jones **53.71%**. A Democratic lead in the Madison subtotal therefore coexists with relative Republican overperformance in the legislative contest. [HD-25 map](maps/hd25.png).

**SD-2: a favorable Madison electorate masks the largest benchmark shortfall.** Drake’s 56.95% Madison subtotal is substantial, yet Drake trails Wess in **all 22** comparable precincts, averaging **−3.65 points**, and trails Jones by **6.74 points**. At Asbury, Drake takes **37.42%**, versus Wess’s **43.38%** and Jones’s **47.60%**. At Madison Public Library, the corresponding shares are **48.59%, 53.82% and 56.29%**. Roberts’s relative strength is clearest in the competitive group, where Drake trails Wess by **4.00 points**, compared with **2.87** in the strongest Democratic group. [SD-2 map](maps/sd2.png), [coalition strata](coalition-strata.csv).

**SD-7: a near tie built from sharply different precinct blocs.** Sluss is close to Wess in the strongly Democratic group (**−0.66 points**) but farther behind in the competitive group (**−2.28**) and Republican-leaning group (**−2.26**). At Dr. Richard Showers Center, Sluss and Wess both take **94.58%**. At Covenant Presbyterian, Sluss takes **43.05%**, Wess **46.88%**, and Jones **52.66%**. Givhan’s relative advantage is concentrated outside Sluss’s strongest base precincts. [SD-7 map](maps/sd7.png).

The SD-7 administrative subtotal matters unusually much: Sluss leads **28,713–28,599**, or **114 votes**, across geographic precincts. Absentee returns add **1,542–1,079**, or another **463 votes**, producing the overall **577-vote** lead. Absentee votes widen the lead; they do not change the leader. Sluss’s absentee two-party share is **58.83%**, versus **50.10%** across geographic precincts. Neither subtotal is a certification or a demographic explanation. [Candidate precinct votes](candidate-precinct-votes.csv).

## Local offices: similar base, different strength outside it

| Countywide contested office | Democratic candidate | D share | vs Jones | vs Wess |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| District Court 1 | Kimberly Kelley Rucker | 53.78% | −4.38 pp | −1.20 pp |
| District Court 4 | Jason M. Jones | 53.79% | −4.38 pp | −1.20 pp |
| District Court 5 | Raven Beach | 53.53% | −4.64 pp | −1.46 pp |
| Sheriff | Brett Jones | 52.97% | −5.13 pp | −1.95 pp |
| Tax collector | Jeff Taylor | 52.91% | −5.26 pp | −2.08 pp |

All five comparisons use all 79 geographic precincts. Their geographic weighted differences and their administrative-inclusive headline shares have different denominators, as described above. [Local contested overview](03-local-contested.png), [ticket comparison chart](05-ticket-comparison.png).

Rucker and Jason M. Jones are almost indistinguishable countywide: their two-party shares differ by just **0.012 percentage points**. Both outperform the other three local Democrats on the Wess benchmark, although all five trail Wess. Sheriff and tax collector both support the Democrat in **47 of 79 geographic precincts**, versus 50 for Wess. Brett Jones trails Wess in **76 precincts** and Taylor in **74**. [Precinct comparisons](precinct-comparisons.csv).

The gaps are particularly revealing in the competitive Senate group: Brett Jones takes **49.01%** there, and Taylor **48.77%**, even as Wess takes **51.23%**. Rucker and Jason M. Jones also fall just below 50% in that group. Their overall leads depend on stronger Democratic precincts and administrative votes overcoming competitive-area deficits. In the strongest Democratic group, Rucker trails Wess by only **0.50 points**, compared with **1.54 points** in the competitive group. This is a pattern of a common base with varying reach beyond it, rather than entirely different geographic coalitions. [Coalition-strata data](coalition-strata.csv).

The school races cannot be treated as equivalent countywide electorates. Keith Trawick leads E. Quinn Headen **30,266–27,109**, while Brian Brooks leads Austin Jones **6,010–2,507** in school board district 3. Their ballot coverage differs from the Governor/Senate electorate within some reporting precincts. The maps therefore label top-ticket differences **context only** and exclude both races from the candidate-overperformance chart. Whole reporting precinct shapes are displayed, not asserted legal school boundaries. [Superintendent map](maps/school-superintendent.png), [school board map](maps/county-boe-3.png).

The five unopposed local offices are mapped separately as named-candidate share of all contest votes, retaining write-ins. Their results cannot support the same coalition inference as competitive D/R races. The local amendment receives **87,663 Yes to 52,245 No**, or **62.66% Yes**; its map is nonpartisan. [Unopposed overview](04-local-uncontested.png), [local amendment map](maps/madison-local-amendment.png).

## Method, reproducibility and limits

1. **Preserve observed returns.** Keep the original summary, details, settings, status, provider map and accepted normalized batch; verify SHA-256 hashes. Each candidate’s precinct sum reproduces the official summary. All 49 contests are checked, although 22 are rendered. Straight-party choices are never added to candidate votes.
2. **Join identities exactly.** Match current official precinct names to the same election’s prepared provider polygons. There are 79 unique geographic names and three administrative names: ABSENTEE, Provisional and PROVISIONAL ABSENTEE. Join cardinality is one-to-one. Validity and completeness checks run before reprojection to NAD83 / UTM zone 16N, EPSG:26916.
3. **Keep administrative ballots separate.** Include them in headline race totals and candidate CSVs; exclude them from geographic comparisons. Zero provisional rows do not establish that provisional counting is complete.
4. **Withhold split-precinct benchmarks.** A geographic name appearing in multiple House or Senate contests in the complete Madison roster is a split name: 21 House names and 10 Senate names. A legislative candidate’s subset cannot be compared directly with whole-precinct Governor votes. Such comparisons are missing/hatched, not allocated by area. This roster rule is conservative and identifies known chamber splits; it does not independently certify legal boundaries.
5. **Define the comparison.** For each eligible precinct, calculate `100 × D_race/(D_race+R_race) − 100 × D_benchmark/(D_benchmark+R_benchmark)`. Average these differences using `D_race+R_race` weights. Show both Governor and Senate benchmarks. Do not compare statewide or countywide shares with a smaller district share as though geography were held fixed.
6. **Separate result maps from comparative inference.** Legislative shapes use the existing district-clipped display reference; clipping does not split or redistribute vote counts. Detail panels share one extent within each race; overview sheets and the interactive reader use a common county extent. Grey indicates no usable comparison/return, and hatching identifies withheld chamber splits. School differences are contextual. Unopposed contests and Yes/No measures do not receive D/R comparisons.
7. **Interpret geography cautiously.** These are complete aggregate observations for this published snapshot, not a random voter sample. There are no demographic joins, individual ballot records, causal campaign estimates or estimates of voter transitions. Precinct populations, candidate-specific participation and ballot eligibility can differ. Spatial similarity cannot establish identical individual coalitions. No historical swing or 2024 allocation is used.

Reproduce from the project root:

```bash
.venv/bin/python scripts/create-madison-2026-general-atlas.py
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_madison_2026_general_atlas.py -q
```

The renderer is entirely offline and leaves the running election dashboard untouched. Source files are under `alabama/data/madison-2026-general-atlas`; the task record is `alabama/research/madison-2026-general-atlas/TASK.md`. External retrieval was attempted: Firecrawl had exhausted credits; direct HTTP/web readers returned 403. The already-running validated official collector successfully retrieved the revision, and its original timestamps and raw entities were preserved through read-only access. This report does not claim an independent second download of the same official source.

Software: GeoPandas 1.1.4, Pandas 3.0.5, Matplotlib 3.11.1, Shapely 2.1.2 in the existing Election-Maps environment. Verification evidence is retained in [verification.json](verification.json); browser and artifact QA are recorded separately after rendering.

This bundle compares 2020 presidential and House results with 2024 House results on the 27-precinct Pennsylvania House District 12 geography; 14 precincts meet the stable comparable-geometry rule.

The scripts use the 2020 MEDSL precinct archive, the 2020 Butler precinct GeoPackage, the 2024 Pennsylvania precinct CSV, and the HD-12 2026 special-election derived geometry listed with checksums in `map_spec.json`.

The result is a precinct-level comparison between different elections, not an individual-level transition or causal estimate. PDF extraction, exact vote-pair joins, and the 2024 boundary vintage constrain interpretation; the displayed denominator is two-party votes.

Precinct winner and lead using the established Alabama two-candidate palette,
white background and ten-percentage-point bands (60+ top band). The revised plate
follows the latest AL-02 masthead, wikibox-style results table and precinct-detail
layout. The main map has no geographic labels; one Charleston inset shows detail.
Interior county lines come from the separate administrative boundary layer. The
state outline uses only exterior rings of the displayed precinct footprint, so
internal coverage holes do not create black seams or shift the coastline.

The companion Andrews–Norman map combines a bivariate precinct map with a scatterplot.
Its predictor is Norman's share of the **August 11 special Republican primary**,
using all ten candidates in the denominator. The August 25 runoff is retained as a
separate sensitivity check; the June primary did not include Norman. See `relationship-analysis.md` for
results, denominators, exclusions, sensitivity checks and limitations.

The baseline map shows only **Trump's 2024 two-party share minus Graham's 2026
two-party share**. Darker blue marks larger losses in fixed five-point bands;
the map has no Norman encoding, scatterplot or table. It includes every valid
general-election comparison, regardless of whether its primary had votes.
Tan indicates a gain and gray indicates no comparable boundary or votes.
It uses only precinct footprints with at least 98% intersection-over-union

Only the selected county group is drawn, with both panels fitted

Compact area results beneath each panel give candidate votes and runoff shares,

# Congressional Midterm Counterfactual

[PNG](southern-midterm-congressional-scenario.png) ·
[SVG](southern-midterm-congressional-scenario.svg) ·
[District results](district-results.csv) ·
[Precinct allocation audit](precinct-district-allocation-audit.csv)

The existing five-state hypothetical 2026 midterm scenario, aggregated into the
38 congressional districts used for the 2026 election (120th Congress). Original
precinct margin shading and precinct lines remain; heavier boundaries and numbered
labels identify districts. The table gives modeled two-party Democratic and
Republican percentages, margins, and the resulting state seat counts. Large
statewide results retain their previous geographic anchors.

The [statewide/demographic version](../alabama-mississippi-2026-midterm-scenario/README.md)
remains available. This congressional version uses exactly the same modeled
precinct votes; it does not refit the hypothetical or introduce candidate effects.

## District boundaries

Official Census 2026 TIGER/Line CD120 files, downloaded October 29, 2026. These
include the updated Alabama and Louisiana plans. The older congressional splits
in the 2024 precinct archives are not used. [Census documentation](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial-census/about/rdo/congressional-districts.120th_Congress.html)
reports that none of these five states' 120th Congress districts split a 2020
Census block. Each populated block's Census internal point therefore identifies
its district without estimating a division within the block.

## Allocation

Reuse the parent model's 2020 Census P3 voting-age-population counts and block
assignments to 2024 precincts: Mississippi's source block equivalency first;
otherwise unique within-precinct joins constrained to the block's source county.
The parent method permits unique county-constrained nearest matches within 1 km;
none were needed in these five states. Georgia's source county-code repairs from
the parent model are retained.

All positive-VAP blocks join uniquely within a 2026 congressional district;
no nearest-district matching or area weighting is used. For each precinct p and
district c:

`weight(p,c) = sum(block VAP assigned to p and c) / sum(block VAP assigned to p)`

Multiply each parent precinct's modeled D/R and baseline D/R votes by this same
weight. Thus the two pieces of a split precinct retain the parent's modeled vote
split; only their vote counts change. The map continues to shade original
precincts, with district boundaries drawn over them.

Precincts with no assigned block VAP are assigned in full only when their complete
polygon is covered by a single district. A positive-vote precinct without block
VAP that crosses a district boundary is an error. Zero-vote, zero-VAP precincts
crossing district lines carry zero weights/votes, with their geometry retained.
Every precinct, county and state is reconciled against its parent baseline and
modeled votes. Allocation metadata records all exceptions.

## Interpretation

VAP is a population proxy for allocating unobserved subprecinct votes, not a
verified count of voters. This assumes the same party split and participation
across pieces of each precinct. Population changes since 2020 and local candidate
or incumbency effects are not estimated. Race and education inputs in the parent
scenario are survey estimates, not certified demographic results. This is a
hypothetical scenario, not a forecast.

`district-results.csv` also includes `turnout_pct_of_2024`: modeled two-party voters
as a percentage of the allocated 2024 two-party baseline, not an absolute
eligible-population turnout rate. Percentages in the image's D/R table are vote
shares; margins are percentage points.

## Rebuild

With the existing parent precinct GeoPackage, PL sources, original precinct
archives, and five Census CD120 ZIPs staged at paths recorded in provenance:

```sh
.venv/bin/python scripts/create-southern-midterm-congressional-map.py
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_southern_midterm_congressional.py tests/test_alabama_mississippi_midterm.py tests/test_alabama_2026_governor_rendering.py tests/test_cartography.py tests/test_output_contract.py
.venv/bin/election-maps validate-outputs outputs/southern-2026-midterm-congressional-scenario
```

Raw archives are preserved. Full block membership CSV and district-result
GeoPackage are reconstructable local products below
`mississippi/data/alabama-midterm-comparison/`, not publication artifacts. Source
hashes, code hashes, versions, CRS, predicates and conservation evidence are in
`provenance.json` and `allocation-audit.json`. The durable task checklist is in
the parent bundle's `TASK.md`.

## Verification

## Revised 2024 two-party Harris support

| State | Black | White | Other / unclassified | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| AL | 99.50% | 12.19% | 99.10% | Bootstrap median |
| AR | 86.44% | 21.51% | 79.12% | Imputed survey adjustment |
| GA | 94.18% | 22.23% | 93.04% | Imputed survey adjustment |
| LA | 97.54% | 13.08% | 69.46% | Bootstrap median |
| MS | 89.16% | 4.84% | 42.93% | Bootstrap median |
| NC | 94.76% | 29.30% | 84.11% | Bootstrap median |
| SC | 95.05% | 23.45% | 76.09% | Bootstrap median |
| TN | 95.19% | 20.21% | 78.93% | Imputed survey adjustment |
| VA | 95.19% | 37.83% | 96.91% | Imputed survey adjustment |

The equal-state median additive adjustments are **+8.3186 percentage points Black, −7.0661 points White, +34.4869 points residual**. These are changes in Democratic vote share, so the associated D-minus-R margin changes are twice as large. They are applied to the missing states’ two-party survey splits, clipped to 0.1–99.9%. The residual survey preference is inferred from the observed state total and rounded Black/White survey shares; this extrapolation is particularly weak. Each donor state contributes equally, including Alabama as requested.

The [underlying refit](../southern-2024-turnout-constrained-racial-estimates/README.md) uses official racial participation in AL/LA/NC/SC and L2 modeled ethnicity in MS. These are **ecological candidate-choice estimates, not verified racial vote counts**. Alabama’s Black/residual fits and Mississippi’s White fit are boundary-sensitive. Bootstrap medians and geographic resampling bands are conditional on the source allocation and model; they do not resolve systematic identification errors. No error bands are propagated into this point scenario.

## Accounting and geography

Independent medians of the three racial preferences need not reproduce a state’s actual Harris share when combined with observed racial composition. To keep every requested median fixed, the model minimally adjusts racial electorate shares by an exponential tilt, minimizing relative entropy from the supplied composition subject to the observed 2024 state vote. The largest composition change in fitted states is under 0.25 percentage points. In imputed states it reaches **5.50 points** (Arkansas White share); those composition shifts are additional modeling assumptions. Both original and reconciled shares are recorded in `baseline-assumptions.csv`.

Three-group, party-specific iterative proportional fitting preserves every precinct’s observed Harris/Trump totals and each state’s reconciled racial party totals. Geographic priors use the participation-constrained precinct composition for the five fitted states and 2020 Census race-alone VAP elsewhere. This uses local turnout composition but applies statewide preference medians; it does not reuse county-specific preference fits. The original FEC-calibrated 2024 precinct party baselines are unchanged.

The Mississippi endpoint remains **D+0.5**, with **96% Black Democratic support**, anchored to the previously selected Presley estimate. Turnout occurs first and accounts for one-third of Mississippi’s Democratic share gain; persuasion accounts for two-thirds. 85% of 2024 Democratic voters and 72.1596% of Republican voters return. Of returning Republican voters, 57.2254% of Black voters and 10.7044% of non-Black voters cross to Democrats. The two racial crossover rates are applied throughout the region; resulting percentage-point swings differ with each state’s starting support. These are hypothetical parameters.

`turnout_pct_of_2024` means modeled two-party voters divided by the same unit’s 2024 two-party voters, **not absolute turnout among eligible or registered voters**. Race and education turnout/results are in `demographic-results-audit.csv`. Education contrasts and partition weights remain survey based, recalibrated to the revised racial medians; no independent education or income persuasion effect is estimated.

`create-tennessee-2016-2024-presidential-swing-map.py` transfers 2016 votes through a spatial crosswalk to 2024 precincts, computes `2024 Harris two-party share − 2016 Clinton two-party share`, and renders fixed diverging classes centered at zero.
